subtopic: LAKE ST. JOHN PULP AND PAPER COMPANY PLANT AT DOLBEAU, P.Q.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. LOUIS S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, on
the 5th of March the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) read to the house a letter addressed to him on March 3 by Mr. L. Dumais, secretary of the National Catholic Union of the pulp and paper industry, of Dolbeau, informing him that a pulp and paper company had carried on manufacturing operations at that place on Sunday, May 1. The hon. member asked whether the Minister of Justice would take immediate steps to ensure the observance of the law prohibiting Sunday labour.
Mr. Dumais' letter refers to a communication from the Department of Justice addressed to Mr. P. J. Martel of Chicoutimi on January 21 last, informing him that the government had not passed any order in council amending the Lord's Day Act. In this letter the deputy minister of justice added that he had no personal knowledge of the paper industry having been classed as an essential war industry.
It would be a complete answer to the hon. member's question to point out to him that the administration of justice is a provincial matter and that the Lord's Day Act expressly states that no action or prosecution for a violation of the act shall be commenced without the leave of the attorney general for the province in which the offence is alleged

Sunday Labour
to have been committed. However, believing that the hon. member wished to obtain the fullest possible information on the point, not only for himself but for all those who are interested in the question of Sunday observance, I have endeavoured to procure it for him.
The hon. member knows that, notwithstanding the general provisions of the act, section 11 allows the performance on Sunday of any "work of necessity or mercy." In paragraphs (a) to (x) of section 11 various kinds of work are given as examples. Since the outbreak of the war the question has frequently arisen whether the urgent need of certain products was sufficient reason to continue their manufacture on Sundays. So long as the dominion government has not made any specific enactment in the matter, each case is one for the attorney general of the province to decide when, an apparent violation of the act having occurred, he is requested to authorize the taking of an action or a prosecution in the premises. Should he allow proceedings to be taken, the courts will decide the issue.
I am informed that in many instances manufacturers pressed by the Department of Munitions and Supply to increase their output have asked that department whether, in order to do so, they would be allowed to carry on their work on Sundays. Of course, the Department of Munitions and Supply could not give a certificate of immunity to anybody, but the officers of that department could express their opinion as to whether or not the work in question was sufficiently urgent to be classified as "work of necessity or mercy." I am told that in many instances officers of that department have written to manufacturers letters expressing an affirmative opinion and that the bearers of such letters communicated them to the attorney general of the province in which their plants were situated, who accepted the opinion of the Department of Munitions and Supply as sufficient reason for the exercise by him of the discretionary power to deny authorization to prosecute, conferred upon him by section 16 of the act.
I do not know whether or not the company operating the pulp and paper plant at Dolbeau has obtained from the Department of Munitions and Supply a statement of opinion as to the urgency of increasing the volume of its production, but I know in a general way that, wishing to accelerate as much as possible the output of pulp and paper, that department has informed several manufacturers that it considered the urgency sufficiently great to justify their requesting the attorney general
of their province not to authorize proceedings against them in respect of work done on Sundays for the purpose of increasing available stocks of their product.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.
He said: For the greater part of the past decade wheat has been a difficult and an extremely complicated problem for the dominion government. It has been possible to decide upon each year's programme only after weighing all the factors capable of measurement or accurate appraisal. For several months now this government has given very serious consideration to all phases of our present wheat position and I can say frankly that the decision this year has had to be made in the face of the most difficult set of circumstances which has, I believe, ever confronted this country in regard to wheat.
In arriving at our decision we have most carefully considered the various representations which have been made to us by different groups from the western provinces and have been in almost continuous consultation with advisers of the government as well as between members of the wheat committee of the cabinet and of the whole cabinet. This has resulted in a most comprehensive research into the whole wheat situation. The many recommendations we have received have been carefully analysed and the present decisions have only been arrived at after the most thoughtful consideration of every angle of the problem.

Five major factors have had to be considered. These factors were:
(1)	The necessary steps to be taken to improve the position of wheat producers who constitute such a large and important group in Canada, and on whom in large measure depend the well-being of the economy of the prairie provinces as well as of Canada as a whole.
(2)	The extent to which the dominion government could act in respect to the wheat problem without detracting from our immediate objectives in respect to the war.
(3)	The extent to which we could count on export markets during 1942-43.
(4)	The responsibility which we bear to ourselves and to our allies in this war in maintaining a reserve of wheat in Canada sufficient to meet unforeseen contingencies.
(5)	The relative importance of wheat production in 1942 as compared to other farm products under the stress of wartime conditions.
While other factors entered1 into our consideration of our present wheat problem, these five factors emerge as the most significant in relation to the decision which the dominion government had to make. Let me deal briefly with each of these points.
In regard to the position of the wheat industry and wheat producers in the prairie provinces, the government has throughout its consideration of 1942-43 wheat policy, been very sympathetic to, and in fact strongly in favour of additional financial support to wheat producers and the western economy through an enlarged income from wheat. This decision in itself was not difficult to make because the government has been aware that wheat prices were low when Canada entered the present war, and since the outbreak of the war the fixed initial price of wheat under the Canadian Wheat Board Act has been continued at 70 cents per bushel No. 1 northern in store Fort William and Vancouver. Additional assistance in 1941-42 does not alter the government's attitude toward the price of wheat. During these war years production costs have increased for the wheat producer as for practically all primary producers in Canada, and therefore, it is only reasonable that at the proper time an adjustment should be made in the income derived from the production of wheat.
As far as this government is concerned, the only question in regard to this phase of the wheat problem was by how much and in what manner it would be possible to improve the income of wheat producers with due regard to the other obligations of the government in respect to the all-important question of the

Wheat Board Act
successful prosecution of the war. No one in Canada, and certainly not the wheat producers of the prairie provinces, suggest that anything should be done in respect to wheat which will in any way limit the capacity of this government to meet the immediate responsibilities and burdens of the war.
In connection with the second point we have had to carefully examine the possibilities of moving our wheat into export trade. Under existing conditions, export markets for Canadian wheat are definitely limited; that is inevitable in the present phase of the war. Our principal market last year was, and this year will be the United Kingdom, and in forecasting our export possibilities we can only see in sight the immediate requirements of the British isles, and rather small exports to other countries.
The government has kept in mind at all times, in addition to these immediate considerations, the more general responsibility which Canada must assume in respect to providing adequate reserves of wheat for the United Kingdom, and our allies and against possible contingencies. At the end of last July Canada had a carryover of 480 million bushels of wheat, in all positions, the largest year-end stock of wheat ever held by this
country. We expect to have about 400 million bushels of wheat on hand at the end of the present crop year, or when the 1942 crop is ready for harvest. The government believes that this stock of wheat constitutes an adequate reserve of Canadian wheat, and does not feel that Canada can be called upon to maintain wartime reserves in excess of this amount. If we maintain a reserve in these proportions we are doing all that can be expected of us at this stage of the war. In addition to the reserves of wheat which we shall hold in Canada on July 31st next, the United States will have the largest carryover in its history-slightly over 600 million bushels-and it is estimated that Argentina and Australia will hold stocks of 360 million bushels. At the end of next July, the four chief wheat exporting countries will have a carryover of 1,300,000,000 bushels of wheat in addition to the surpluses which may arise from 1942 production. In the face of this situation there should be no anxiety as to the supplies of wheat available in normally exporting countries, and in particular in Canada and the United States.

This cannot be said, however, in respect to practically all other farm products produced in the prairie provinces. We urgently need more hogs; we urgently need more feed grains; we urgently need more milk, butter and cheese. If the government were to establish priorities in respect to the production of farm products in 1942, it would be necessary to place wheat well down on the list, topped1 in point of urgency by feed grains, live stock and live stock products. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, will be dealing with the coarse grain situation but the situation is a most vital one and had to be considered along with our wheat policy. I stress this point deliberately in order to make it clear .that an undue expansion in wheat acreage and wheat production in 1942 is not advisable, and at the same time to strongly urge every producer in the prairie provinces to make certain that the government's wheat policy does not influence him one iota to cease, or in any way interfere with his efforts to increase feed grain and live stock production to the limit of his resources.
When the full grain programme for 1942 is before the house it will -be seen that the government has made provision for encouraging farm production along the lines most urgently required, and provision will be made whereby wheat producers may benefit from the 1942-43 wheat programme without unduly expanding wheat acreage.
Before dealing with the 1942-43 programme, I -would like to briefly review the wheat position in the present crop year, 1941-42.
As I have already noted, Canada ended the crop year 1940-41 with a carryover of 480 million 'bushels (on July 31, 1941). This was a smaller carryover than we had expected- to have earlier in that crop year as it seemed inevitable that our carryover on July 31, 1941, would be about 550 million bushels. As a result of increased exports, mainly in April,

Kingdom, total exports in 1940-41 amounted to 230 million bushels, whereas we had expected exports, at best, of about ISO million bushels. This increase in exports to the United Kingdom, substantial flour exports to Britain and other countries, and a somewhat larger domestic demand for wheat made it possible for us to bring our July 31 carryover down to the 480 million bushel level.
The 1941 wheat crop in the -prairie provinces and in Ontario was very small. Canadian production in 1941 is now estimated at 299 million bushels, as compared with 540 million bushels harvested in 1940. Despite this the wheat problem has persisted in a very difficult form. The following figures show the quantities of -wheat available in Canada in 1940 and 1941:

million bushels of wheat with which to deal in 1940-41, after harvesting the second largest crop in history. During the present crop year we have had 779 million bushels of wheat with which to deal after harvesting a relatively small crop. These statistics show that the increase in carryover between July 31, 1940 and July 31st, 1941, largely offset decreased production in 1941. In spite of the small crop in 1941 we have only 62 million bushels less wheat to handle during the present crop year, as compared with the previous crop year when production was so high. The house will appreciate from these statistics the extent of the wheat problem for which we had to prepare, and for which we were prepared, in 1941-42. If the 1941 wheat crop had been 400 million bushels instead of 299 million bushels, we would have had to deal with nearly 900 million bushels of wheat during the present crop year. If yields of 1940 had been repeated in 1941, we would have had to deal with over a -billion bushels of wheat in Canada.
One of the effects of the small crop harvested in 1941 was to materially ease the grain storage problem in Canada, and the Canadian wheat board was able to rapidly advance delivery quotas during the fall of 1941. The crop year commenced with a general delivery quota of 5 bushels per authorized acre; on -October 7th the general quota was raised to 8 bushels per authorized acre; on October 16th to 12 bushels per authorized acre; and on November 21st to 15 bushels per authorized acre. Finally, on December 6th, quotas were removed and all delivery points in the prairie

Wheat Board Act
provinces were placed on an "open delivery'' basis. In addition to the ' increases in the general quota, the delivery quotas at individual stations were raised throughout the fall months as soon as local storage permitted.
The dominion government undertook to limit deliveries in all of Canada to 230 million bushels, which would mean about 223 million bushels deliverable in the prairie provinces. Since the prairie wheat crop amounted to 279 million bushels in 1941, it was apparent from the commencement of the new crop year, that marketings would not exceed the maximum established by the dominion government, making it possible to take delivery of all surplus wheat in the prairie provinces. It is expected that total deliveries for the crop year 1941-42 will amount to about 200 million bushels, which will be well within the limit prescribed for the prairie provinces.
Up until February 27th country deliveries of wheat had amounted to 166 million bushels, leaving a balance of about 34 million bushels to be delivered before July 31st, 1942.
Exports are running somewhat higher than for the corresponding period of 1940-41. Up to February 27th export clearances of wheat had amounted to 84 million bushels as compared with 65 million bushels for the corresponding period of last year. In addition during the six months ending January, flour exports in terms of wheat had amounted to 22 million bushels this crop year, as compared with 15 million bushels for the same months in 1940-41. It may be said, therefore, that our exports of wheat and flour are running about 25 million bushels ahead of the same period in 1940-41. We must remember, however, that exports were very light up to this time a year ago, and did not run into substantial volume until the last four months of the crop year. As the crop year progresses, therefore, it is very likely that our exports will be less favourable as compared with a year ago. I would not attempt to forecast our wheat exports for the crop year 1941-42 because the volume of these exports depends so largely upon the requirements of the United Kingdom and the ability to provide the necessary shipping.
In announcing the government's 1942-43 wheat programme, I shall deal with that part of the programme which comes within the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Following my statement, my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), will deal with other forms of assistance which will be administered by his department.
I wish to make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that the announcements to be made by my
colleague and this announcement by me are closely related. There are not two plans but one plan carefully worked out, each in relation to the other on the basis of the needs as w'e see them of the whole of the western provinces.
In so far as the wheat programme is concerned, no attempt has been made to formulate a long term policy. This would be virtually impossible in the light of the many factors which have a direct bearing on our policy at the present time but which may or may not exist after the cessation of hostilities. In the studies which have been made in regard to the whole agricultural policy to be followed in the west, a possible long term programme has been reviewed but, as I say, under present circumstances it is not possible to implement a programme which might be dislocated within six months of its announcement.
It is my responsibility to announce the government's decision in respect to the price which will be paid to the farmers for wheat in 1942-43, the volume of wheat which we propose to accept in that crop year and decisions which have been made in regard to price of certain coarse grains and flaxseed.
The government proposes that the fixed initial price for wheat delivered in 1942-43 under authorized delivery quotas shall be 90 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 northern wheat in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver.
In reaching its decision in regard to the fixed price per bushel of wheat, the government has taken into account the position of producers who, by virtue of geographical location, and established farm practice, must depend mainly upon wheat production in their farm operations. Producers in this position have not been able to take as much advantage as producers in other areas of remunerative markets which have existed for live stock and live stock products. With due regard to the percentage of total wheat acreage in the prairie provinces which is normally seeded to wheat in these areas, the government feels that an increase in the per bushel price is an effective way of assisting those who need assistance most.
It is not the intention of the government that domestic buyers of wheat and wheat products shall be deprived of the protection of the price control policy.
Accordingly, the Canadian wheat board will continue to sell wheat to domestic buyers for flour or other use at a price which conforms to the spirit and intention of the maximum prices regulations and is an appropriate price in relation to the domestic selling prices of goods made from wheat or in the production of which wheat is used.
The wartime prices and trade board, in the discharge of its responsibilities under the maxi-
Wheat Board Act

mum prices regulations and the wartime prices and trade regulations, will have the duty of determining the price at which wheat will be sold to domestic buyers in accordance with these principles.
The wartime prices and trade board will discharge this duty from time to time after consultation with the Canadian wheat board.
Since the resolution on the order paper on March 5 indicated an increase in the fixed initial price of wheat, the Canadian wheat board has taken steps to prevent any speculative profits that might arise from the government's decision and to that end sent the following wire to the secretary of the Winnipeg grain exchange before the opening of the market on March 6:

In announcing the government's decision in regard to price, I may once again reiterate the fact that this new price is not to be considered as warranting undue expansion in wheat acreage. I will go one step further. This is the highest government-guaranteed price for Canadian wheat at any time since the last war. Wheat producers must accept the responsibility of keeping wheat acreage at reasonable levels.
In proposing a price of 90 cents per bushel for No. 1 northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver, the government is going as far as it feels it can go, with due regard to its immediate and unprecedented financial responsibilities in connection with the prosecution of the war. I need not remind this house of the present financial commitments of the government in respect to wheat. The annual report of the Canadian wheat board, recently tabled in this house, showed on July 31. 1941, deficits in respect to 1938, 1939 and 1940 crops amounting to 879,972,814.45. A substantial proportion of Canadian wheat supplies is held by the Canadian wheat board and is a direct responsibility of the dominion government.
In addition to these exceedingly large commitments in respect to wheat, the new fixed price will add materially to the government's obligations in respect to wheat during 1942-43.
In addition to increasing the fixed price per bushel of wheat, the government proposes to substantially increase authorized deliveries of wheat in the prairie provinces and British Columbia during 1942-43 to a total of 280 million bushels.
This figure is based upon estimated domestic and export demand but it is extremely difficult to accurately forecast exports a year and a half in advance. The government is guided by estimates of exports and domestic demand and is fixing authorized deliveries at 280 million bushels. This figure will not be changed on the' basis of later estimates of the 1942-43 demand for Canadian wheat. The government thinks it is more satisfactory from the producers' standpoint to name a definite figure for marketings in 1942-43, rather than make it conditional upon factors which can only be estimated.
The authorized deliveries of 280 million bushels will apply only to the prairie provinces and part of British Columbia. The government does not propose to regulate marketings in eastern Canada because of the large demand

Wheat Board Act
for soft wheat for milling purposes, and because of the volume of grain required for live stock feeding in eastern Canada.
In the main, the government's proposal to permit marketings of 280 million bushels in the prairie provinces and British Columbia during 1942-43 was designed to limit such marketings to about the quantity which will go into export trade or domestic consumption in Canada. As a result, the government does not anticipate much change in year-end stocks on July 31, 1943, as compared with stocks which will be carried on July 31, 1942.
Delivery Quotas.-As long as maximum authorized deliveries are established for the prairie provinces, it will be necessary to provide for the limitation of farm deliveries. This is the only way in which total deliveries may be regulated.
The government, in consultation with the Canadian wheat board, proposes that individual deliveries in the prairie provinces and British Columbia will be based upon authorized acreage of each individual producer, as established in 1941-42. On this basis the authorized acreage of the prairie provinces and British Columbia for delivery purposes will be about 20,000,000 acres.
The per-bushel quotas to be estimated on authorized acreage in 1942-43 will be determined in an equitable manner when 1942 seeded acreages are known and when the general pattern of the 1942 crop is established. It is the desire of the government and the board that the simplest possible quota plan be established for 1942-43, consistent with the obligation of distributing marketings of 280 million bushels equitably among approximately 240,000 wheat farmers in the prairie provinces.
In connection with establishing delivery quotas it will be necessary for all wheat producers who are operating new farms in 1942; or who are operating more land in 1942 than in 1941; or who are operating less land in 1942 than in 1941; or who did not take out permits in 1941, to advise the Canadian wheat board at the earliest possible moment of changes in their farms or of the fact that they do not hold 1941 permits. This is necessary in order that authorized acreages may be properly established and in order that there be as little delay as possible in issuing permits to deliver wheat in 1942-43.
Before leaving the matter of the price of wheat for 1942-43, and authorized marketings, I would like to indicate broadly the effect of the new price upon potential income in the prairie provinces. I say "potential" for the reason that we cannot be assured of how much wheat will be produced in 1942-43 when the new price basis becomes effective. In 1941-42
the dominion government permitted the marketing of 230 million bushels, which at the fixed price of 70 cents per bushel provided for farm income from wheat of about $125,000,000. Since a very short crop was harvested in 1941, wheat deliveries will probably not exceed 200 million bushels, and the return to wheat producers will be about $106,000,000, exclusive of other forms of assistance.
In raising the per-bushel return from wheat and the amount of wheat permitted to be marketed from 230 million bushels to 280 million bushels, the potential wheat income of the prairie provinces will be raised from $125,000,000 in 1941-42 to about $205,000,000 in 1942-43, provided the full amount of the authorized marketings is available. The government's proposals in connection with price and authorized marketings therefore involve a very substantial increase in the income of wheat producers. When this increase in income from wheat is placed alongside of a very large income which is now accruing to producers of the prairie provinces from the sale of live stock, live-stock products, and grains other than wheat, western Canada should be assured of a very substantial farm income in 1942-43 provided crop conditions are reasonably good. If farm revenues from sources other than wheat increase moderately and if an average crop is harvested in 1942-43 farm revenues should reach $475,000,000 in the prairie provinces during the coming crop year, as compared with about $350,000,000 in 1941-42, exclusive of direct dominion government subsidies in both years.
So far I have dealt mainly with that phase of the government's grain programme which deals primarily with the desire of the government to increase farm income and add greater security to the position of the wheat producer. I now wish to submit three additional and important proposals for the particular purpose of securing increased production of three farm products which are necessary to our national war effort.
These proposals are:
1.	That a minimum price level for barley be established. This minimum price level will be 60c. per bushel basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur for Winnipeg barley futures as well as for all cash barley, basis No. 2 C.W. 6 row at 60 cents. The Canadian wheat board will be empowered to carry out this policy and regulations will be prepared in due course.
2.	That a minimum price level for oats be established. This minimum price level will be 45 cents per bushel basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur for Winnipeg oats futures as well as for all cash oats, basis No. 2 C.W. at 45 cents. As in the case of
Wheat Board Act

barley the Canadian wheat board will be empowered to administer this policy and Regulations will be issued in due course.
3.	That the price of flaxseed be fixed at $2.25 per bushel basis No. 1 C.W., flaxseed in store Fort William/Port Arthur. The dominion government will empower the Canadian wheat board to purchase and handle all flaxseed delivered by producers in Canada in 1942-43. Trading in futures and cash flax will be stopped on all Canadian markets at some date to be determined. An order in council has been passed which prohibits any person under very heavy penalty from moving flaxseed from any licensed or unlicensed elevator or mill in Canada, and also prohibits any operator of any elevator or mill from utilizing flaxseed without the written authority of the Canadian wheat board. Needless to say there will be no interference with the processing of flaxseed in Canada. In the near future regulations will be issued for the handling of flaxseed under the new plan.
In connection with the minimum prices being established for oats and barley the government wishes to give a measure of assurance and security to those producers who cooperate in producing an ample supply of feed grain in 1942 in a patriotic endeavour to maintain our live stock production at high levels. Producers generally will face the new crop year with the assurance that whatever the production of oats and barley is in 1942, the market will be supported on the basis I have outlined.

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, respecting wheat acreage reduction.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, when the measure
which has just been moved to second reading by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr MacKinnon) and the one which I am about to move to second reading were in the resolution stage, it was arranged in the house that these bills should be brought to the point where they would appear on the order paper for second reading; that statements then would be made by the ministers concerned, and that in the discussion following some leeway would be allowed in order that it might not be necessary to deliver three speeches on the three bills that will be before the house. In accordance with that understanding it is my intention at the moment to discuss the three measures, one of which has been advanced on the order paper for second reading and the other two of which now stand for second reading. I shall try to confine my remarks to matters which may concern one or other of these three bills, as they may relate one to another.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) has just moved the adjournment of the debate on one of these measures. I presume that he and other hon. members are in a position to speak on the second reading of either this or the other bill, that someone will move the adjournment of the debate on this measure in due course, and that we shall attempt as far as possible to have only the one discussion dealing with all matters having to do with the wheat policy.
The action being taken in the house this session in relation to the handling of wheat and other grains is along the line of the policy laid down at the beginning of the war. I mention "other grains" because in his statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce
dealt with the handling not only of wheat but also of coarse grains and flax. The discussion therefore will deal with matters other than wheat. The bill providing for wheat acreage reduction also has to do with the production of coarse grains, so that it will be possible to discuss matters having to do with other farm products as well as wheat.
The action we are now taking is the final step in a policy which was laid down at the beginning of the war and which has been consistently adhered to up to the present time. It was stated then that before every war difficulties developed for agriculture, in countries which finally become involved in the war, and more particularly in countries which are suppliers of food commodities to the nations participating in the war. For that reason we in the Department of Agriculture in Canada have been very much concerned during the last two and a half years in developing the agricultural policy of this country to a point where increased prices and quantity would give reasonable returns to farmers. It was realized that prices of farm products were very low before the war. They were low during the first five-year period of preparation for war in Europe from 1930 to 1934. They were not quite so low during the second five-year period from 1935 to 1939. During the two years since the beginning of war prices have gradually advanced on all farm products excepting wheat. There are reasons why wheat should be the last to advance in price.
It will be remembered that just before war was declared, wheat had reached the low level of about 50 cents a bushel. Immediately following the declaration of war wheat gradually began to advance in price, and continued to do so until the spring of 1940. It reached the level of approximately 90 cents a bushel. After the fall of France, the price of wheat dropped very rapidly to the level of about 60 cents a bushel. That drop occurred in a very few days, and then the government of Canada, through the wheat board, pegged the price at 70 cents a bushel, where it has remained ever since.
I cite these facts with regard to wheat in order to indicate that when it was expected that France would continue in the war and that the battles of this war would be fought on the plains of northern France and in Belgium, as was the case in the last war, it was thought that there would be a fairly rapid advance in the price of wheat and that in due course wheat farmers would obtain reasonable prices for their product. But the war has not developed in that way. Up to the present time we have not been able to choose the battlefields. Our enemy has been choos-
Wheat Acreage Reduction

ing them, and during the period of our preparation we have not been feeding the people we expected to. The result is that there has not been a rise in the demand for wheat, because those great agricultural areas are still producing.
From the very beginning of the war it was realized that if farmers in Canada were to be able to maintain themselves and develop agriculture to the point where it could take its proper place in providing food for allied countries, prices in due course must advance. Very early in the war we embarked upon a policy of trying to establish floors under various farm products. The first product under which we were able to establish a floor was hogs. That floor was established by entering into an agreement with the British government in the fall of 1939, the first fall of the war. The second product under which we were able to establish a floor was cheese; it was established in the spring of 1940, when a price of 14 cents a pound at Montreal was agreed upon with the British government. The third product under which we were able to establish a floor was wheat, when we pegged it at 70 cents in 1940. The fourth product was butter for which in the spring of 1941 we were able to establish a price of approximately 30 cents a pound for that summer. Finally, toward the fall of 1941, we were able to establish a floor under eggs, by making an arrangement with Britain under
which we shipped eggs at 28 cents in certain of the summer months and 32 cents in the winter months, which prices were increased a short time ago to 31 and 35 cents a dozen.
So that down to the fall of 1941 we were able to establish floors for various farm products, and I should like to place on Hansard a table indicating the range of prices which brought about the result I have just indicated. For example, from 1930 to 1934 the average price of wheat was 74-2 cents a bushel. For the next five-year period the average price was 96-5 cents. In 1939-40 the price was 76-5; in 1940-41 it was 74 cents, while the average price for the period from 1926 to 1929 was $1.41-7. I place these prices on record to emphasize the fact that while the prices of farm products have been going up, during the first two years of the war, on an average during the second year of the war they were much lower than the average prices for the period 1926-29.
I have placed on record another set of figures, because they demonstrate something else. We will have in mind the fact that ceiling prices have been placed on certain farm commodities. Those ceiling prices are set out in the tables I have placed on Hansard, and I direct the attention of hon. members particularly to them.
May I make these further comments with respect to the ceiling prices. It will be noted that while the ceiling price for oats has been placed at 51-5 cents, the average for the 1926-29 period was 59-7. The ceiling on barley is 64-8, and the average for the period I have indicated was 73-6. No ceiling prices have been placed on wheat or cattle or hogs. However a ceiling of 35-3 cents has been placed on butter, as compared with 38-2 for the period 1926-29. The ceiling price on cheese is 25 cents, as compared with the average of 18-9 cents for the period indicated. The ceiling on eggs stands at 46 cents, compared with 48-2 cents.
I believe it will be found on examination of these figures that in so far as they have been established on products other than grain the ceiling prices are almost the same as the average prices found in the 1926-29 period. When one takes into consideration the increased volume, it will be realized that these products probably bring a higher net income to the farmer than they did at the average price between 1926-29.
There are certain farm products on which no ceiling prices have been established. In this list are wheat, cattle and hogs. No ceiling has been established upon those products as sold by the farmers; but there has been a ceiling established on beef, on pork, and on bread. Although it is not true of bread, it is true of beef and pork that the ceilings established on these products will make possible a price which will be somewhat higher than the average prices for hogs and cattle in the period 1926-29.
I wish now to make a statement to bring to the attention of hon. members the present position of agriculture. I have been speaking of the condition in which agriculture was at the end of the second year of the war. We are now six months into the third year of the war. May I say that there has been a higher floor placed under farm products since the beginning of the third year of the war. The floor prices for the third year of the war are higher than they were in 1941.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just stated that for wheat the advance or floor is to be 90 cents. That is a much higher advance than we had as a floor under wheat during the first two years of the war. He has also announced that the floor under oats will be 45 cents a bushel. May I point out that down to the present time there has been no floor under oats. This simply assures that any farmer who grows oats, whether in eastern or western Canada, will obtain a price based upon the floor of 45 cents a bushel at Fort William. The floor under barley is now 60 cents. In the past there has been no floor under barley. It will be noted, therefore, that for the third crop year of the war there has been established a floor of 60 cents under barley.
The only floor we have had under beef since the beginning of the war has been the agreement with the United States under which we offer our product to the market in the United States at approximately the United States price, less the reduced duty upon cattle going into that country. During recent weeks and at the present time that has given us a floor under cattle, at Toronto, of $9.90. This price is above the average of the period at which we have been aiming.
The price of hogs is $11.63 at Toronto. This is approximately the level at which we had been aiming under our policy of the first two years. Butter is 35J cents per pound, which is just about three cents below that average level of 1926-29. Cheese is 25 cents per pound, just a little more than six cents above that average level. Eggs are 32 cents, somewhat below that average level of 1926-29. This brings live stock products, on the average, to approximately the 1926-29 level. In the case of flax, which was dealt with to-day, the average price for that period was, I think, $2.05 a bushel, so that the price which will prevail in 1942 of $2.25 is 20 cents a bushel above the average price for the four-year period 1926-29.
Let me repeat that wheat and coarse grains are the two products which we have not yet advanced to prices which bear favourable comparison with the average prices for 192629. The fact that coarse grains have not advanced to the 1926-29 level is not so serious a problem from the point of view of the farmer as is the fact that wheat has not advanced to the level of 1926-29. The reason is that by far the greater part of all coarse grains grown in Canada are fed on the farms where they are grown. Those which are not fed on the farms where they are grown are being transported at the present time from one farm to another, whether it be an adjoining farm or a farm at the other end of Canada.
Wheat Acreage Reduction

If it is a farm at the other end of Canada, the government is paying a very considerable part of the freight rate to move it from the one farm to the other. So that the prices of coarse grains in themselves do not play as important a part in the building up of income for the farmer as do products which are produced through feeding coarse grains, such as, butter, cheese, hogs, cattle, and so on. These products, occupying the position that they do in the price level, make it possible for the farmer to grow coarse grains and dispose of them indirectly at a price which approximates the price of 1926-29.
But the wheat growers are in a different class. They are growing a product which is used largely for the purpose of making bread or for human consumption. The price obtained for this product is the only income which the wheat farmer can obtain for by far the greater part of his investment and labour.
May I say that the prices which I have given to this house do not tell the whole story. When I say that to-day we are producing in Canada more than twice as many hogs as we produced in the last year before the war, you will realize that price does not tell the whole story in relation to the income obtained in Canada from hogs. When I say that there has been an increase in the production of nearly every other farm product since the beginning of the war, you will realize that volume as well as price plays a considerable part in the return which the farmer receives for the things which he has to sell.
The result is that the total farm income for 1941, including assistance given by federal and provincial governments-this includes acreage payments or subsidies paid for the production of hogs in Ontario and1 Nova Scotia, subsidies on cheese in Ontario and Quebec, and premiums paid by this government on cheese-taking all these into consideration, the result is that the total farm income in 1941 was $921 million as compared with an average of $966 million for the four-year period 1926-29. I cite these figures in order to emphasize that our farms across Canada drew an income in 1941 of $921 million as against an average income for the four years at which we have been aiming, namely, 1926 to 1929, of $966 million.

A few more farms were being operated in the 1941 period than in the 1926-29 period. I would ask the house to contrast these returns, including those from wheat farming, along with all others, with wheat itself.
The average annual return for wheat in 1926-29 was $405 million, whereas the return in 1941, including all acreage payments, was only $210 million. That is, the return for wheat in 1941 was just a little more than half the average return in 1926-29. The average annual return for all farm products other than wheat during the 1926-29 period was $561 million, whereas the return in 1941 was $711 million. On the one hand, you have one product produced by the farmers of Canada, the income from which dropped from $405 million to $210 million. On the other hand, you have another set of products produced by the farmers of Canada, the income from which in the same period increased from $561 to $711 million. The annual return per farm in the first period was $795, whereas in 1941 it was S961. These figures leave wheat out of the picture. In other words, the return from products outside wheat in 1941 was better than the return in 1926-29, whereas the return from wheat in 1941 was only a little better than fifty per cent of the return in 1926-29. I should like hon. members to keep this fact in mind when we are dealing with the assistance that is to be given to wheat growers by means of the increase in the advance mentioned a few moments ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and also under the provisions of the two bills to which before I sit down I am going to ask the house to give second reading.
It is to improve the position of the farmer who depends largely upon wheat that the advance on wheat has been increased from 70 to 90 cents. This, however, will only improve the position of the wheat farmer, on 280 million bushels of wheat, being the maximum of which we will receive delivery under the advance of 20 cents per bushel, by an increase in revenue of a maximum of $56 million, which will still leave the wheat farmer at least $176 million below the 1926-29 level. If we add the $20 million which he will receive under wheat

Wheat Acreage Reduction
acreage reduction and the estimated $10 million under prairie farm assistance, he will still be $146 million below the 1926-29 level.
As I say, that part of the farmer's operations which is related to wheat will be down by about $176 million. We are going to try to improve this position by taking two steps. We are going to pay $2 an acre for wheat acreage reduction, which on the basis of our 1941 experience will bring $20 million. You will naturally ask me how that improves the position of the wheat farmer. Well, it would not if the government were prepared to take all the wheat the farmer could grow. But we are saying to him:	No matter how good your
crop is, we are going to take only 280 million bushels of wheat this year. It is quite a common thing in western Canada to produce on the average 15 bushels to the acre, and an average of 15 bushels to the acre on 20 million acres will produce 300 million bushels of wheat. It is possible therefore that if the farmers seeded 29 million acres in wheat, as some estimate they did in 1940, and grew even less than 15 bushels to the acre, they might have a very considerable amount of wheat which during this year they would not be able to market. So that the government is saying to the farmer, "we are prepared to pay $2 an acre for a reduction in wheat acreage, which may net you less income than the wheat would."
I should like to correct an impression that seems to have been abroad throughout Canada during this last year that this government was paying for summer-fallow. This government was not paying for summer-fallow last year. We were paying the farmer to reduce his wheat acreage. The discussion in the house last session by those who were in favour of the policy which was then brought before the house was to the effect that we had an enormous carryover, this was referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, a carryover which induced many of us to say last year that by the end of the crop year 1941-42, on July 31 next, we might have an amount of wheat on hand very much in excess of what the figures now indicate will be carried over. I think there were a few who prophesied a carryover of 700 million bushels, and some prophesied that we might even run close to the billion bushel mark. But with a short crop, and the reduced acreage under the wheat acreage reduction plan of last year, we are going to be down to about 400 million bushels at the end of this present crop year. We helped to bring about that reduction through a wheat acreage reduction policy.
The government still feels that it would be a mistake in this third year of the war to put the wheat acreage back to where it was in 1940. There is a difference of opinion as to what the wheat acreage was in 1940. Statistics have estimated that ;t was something over 27 million acres. The wheat board, I think, basing the figures on their permits, have figured it at something over 29 million acres, and the prairie farm assistance organization of the Department of Agriculture have estimated that the reduction from 1940 was approximately 9 million acres, which would place the total at about 29 million. So that if the wheat board's estimate of the average for 1940 is correct, and if our reduction figure, the actual amount of reduced acreage on which we shall be paying, is correct the wheat acreage at the present time should be somewhere around 20 or 21 million acres. It is the desire of the government this year to attempt to hold it at around 20 or 21 million acres. I want to emphasize that, because I noticed a newspaper article the other day in which it was suggested that the present act raised the proposed acreage from 65 to 80 per cent of 1940. That is not the intention of the present act, nor is it in accordance with the terms of the present act. The 80 per cent in the present act has only to do with farmers who in 1940 put practically all their land into wheat. On those particular farms they are only allowed to start their reduction from 80 per cent and work from there down, to earn the $2 an acre that is paid to those who put their reduced wheat acreage into summer-fallow or into coarse grains. Last year we paid $4 an acre when the acres. Last year we paid $4 an acre when the acreage taken out of wheat was put into summer-fallow, and this year we are paying only $2 an acre. Last year we paid $2 an acre on all coarse grains including flax. This year w'e are paying $2 on all coarse grains excluding flax. In other words we are paying $2 on the rye which was mentioned while the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking, but W'e are not paying $2 on flax because the government is prepared to guarantee a price of $2.25 a bushel for flax which it is hoped will induce the production of all the flax that is required.
It might be asked why we are anxious to have an increase in the production of flax and an increase in the production of coarse grains this year. The reason is found in what has been happening in the war in recent months. We had lengthy discussions last year as to the amount of coarse grains that would be required, and whether we could get rid of all our coarse grains if grown in the
Wheat Acreage Reduction

quantities per acre in which they are sometimes grown. We also had lengthy discussions on the question whether we should increase the production of flax. I think I am correct when I say that the flax which we did produce last year was more than twice the amount required to keep the crushers which we have in Canada running, so that if nothing had happened which we did not expect at that time probably those who were then arguing on the other side would have turned out to be right. But many things have happened. Japan has taken possession of by far the greater part of the areas from which vegetable oils come, and immediately Japan took possession of those areas vegetable oils were not available to the allies. Those allies included all the democracies fighting on our side in this war. The United States will suffer from a shortage of oil, Canada will suffer from a shortage of oil, Great Britain will suffer from a shortage of oil, and so will all t'he other countries fighting on our side. The appeal is made to us to produce animal fats in the northern part of this continent, where it is very difficult to produce vegetable oils. We can produce more flax and soya beans. We ean produce sunflowers from which oil can be taken. But we can produce more animal fats through increasing our hogs and dairy products and even through the production of beef. So we are making an appeal to our people this year, by putting a floor under the price of oats and barley; offering $2 an acre on land converted from wheat to coarse grains in order that we may produce animal fats to take the place of the vegetable oils which for the time being we are not going to be able to get. We are asking for more flax to increase vegetable oils. That is the reason for our action in that regard. It will be realized at once that the proposal does cut down somewhat on the return which the wheat farmer will get from the production of wheat. We are asking him to transfer from the production of wheat into the production of coarse grains and flax and hope he will make up by that means some, if not all, of the $146 million he is still below the average 1926-29 level.
I do not know whether members of the house fully understand the situation in western Canada, but I am quite certain that many of those outside the house who discussed the question and who have not been in that part of the country do not understand the problem which there is in western Canada. If you draw a line from Morden in the southern part of Manitoba straight to Lloydminster, which is on the boundary line between Alberta and Saskatchewan, up near the North Saskatchewan river, and then draw another straight line 
from there down to Calgary, and then from Calgary down to the United States boundary line, you will have mapped out south of that line what is known as the Palliser triangle in which it is difficult to produce anything in great volume except wheat. That is because of the nature of the soil, and because, too, of the climate in that particular area.
The important fact is that a million people are living south of that line. South of that line you have cities such as Regina and Saskatoon in Saskatchewan, and, over in the province of Alberta, Calgary, and many other smaller cities and towns in all the provinces. In that area, too, is a vast agricultural population. It is a greater agricultural area in one block than can be found in any other continuous block in Canada. When people are talking about closing up that area, as some do, they are talking about taking care of a million people; and if they are proposing to take care only of those who are on the farms, and on farms upon which only wheat can be grown to advantage, they are going to be asked to take care of at least half a million people. It is not so easy, therefore, to do as some people seem to suppose. They say, "Let them stop growing wheat while the war is an." But there is no way in which these farmers can make a living unless they can grow wheat, and if they cannot be left where they are they must be taken somewhere else where a living can be found for them.
With that picture in front of us, may I say that it is for these people particularly that twenty cents a bushel has been added to the advance which was placed upon wheat. Of course those who grow wheat in the districts just outside the area to the north will benefit to some extent, but that is not where the great bulk of wheat which flows out of western Canada comes from. It comes from the area to the south. As to the others, they are not only getting the twenty cents a bushel for the limited amount of wheat which they grow, but they are receiving an increased price for their live-stock products; increased returns for their coarse grains, if they have a surplus to sell; and in addition to that, what every farmer in western Canada is proud to do at the present time, they are serving the allies. It was not the $4 an acre which was paid for land taken out of wheat and put into summer-fallow, or the $2 an acre for land which was taken out of wheat and put into coarse grains, which induced the farmers of western Canada to do something which has not been done by any farming population anywhere else in the world either since this war started or before it-to take almost one-third of the acreage out of any one crop and to put

Wheat Acreage Reduction
it to other use. It was not because they were going to make money by doing so-they were not-but because they were told it would help to win the war if they did do it, and they did it for that purpose. As I said last year when we were asking them to do it, it took at least a hundred million dollars out of their pockets, and we did not by any means manage to put all of it back in. We attempted to do so, it is true, but the poor crops of last year made it impossible. Not all of what was taken out went back by any indirect means. But this year again all these fanners are going to rise to the appeal which is made by this house, by the government of Canada, but more particularly by the British government and by the other allied countries by whose side we are fighting, to produce live-stock products in even greater quantity than they were produced last year. We have to do that if we are to meet the programme which has been marked out for us. We are asked to produce 600 million pounds of Wiltshire sides, to be placed at Saint John or Montreal to be shipped to Britain during this third year of the war. That is, we shall have to send each week four times as much as we sent to Britain in each week of the last year before the war.
This will give you some idea of the enormous task which the farmers of Canada have attempted. As you know, the hog year begins on the first of October, so that we are now in the sixth month of the operation, and up to the present time the agreed upon amount has been sent. It is going to be more difficult for them during the months which are ahead, but we believe that the farmers will place that amount of pork products at the harbours of Canada to be shipped to Britain during the summer months, thus bringing the total by the end of the year up to 600 million pounds.
Again we are going to be asked to produce, not for consumption here but for shipment to Britain, 125 million pounds of cheese, and the British and Canadian governments will agree on the price to be paid for it. I am not in a position to-day to announce the price, because the negotiations between this country and Great Britain are now proceeding, but it will be a price which will induce a production in Canada during the third summer of the war of at least 125 million pounds of cheese for the British market. You know what that means. It is 25 million pounds more than Canada produced in 1935. and it required more than we have produced in any year since 1925. Our production of cheese had been on the downgrade ever since the last war, but during the last five or six years it has been on the upgrade, and this year we shall send much more cheese to Britain than we produced only a few years ago.
We are not asked to send butter, but we have been requested to ship canned milk. That will be forwarded in increased volume. More and more of the food products of this country will be sent to Britain, but more particularly products which carry animal fats, to take the place of the vegetable oils which cannot now be obtained from other parts of the world, and thus assist in feeding the British people and contribute to the winning of the war.
The legislation-and by the way, it is not all legislation; some of these measures which were placed before you this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be carried out by order in council under the War Measures Act - assists toward that end. It will have the effect of giving a higher return to the farmers in the area from which most of our grain crops come. The regulations which will be enacted by order in council will also assist in the production of coarse grains, and of flax, from which vegetable oil can be taken. The measures which I have placed before you will have the effect of encouraging also the production of coarse grains and hence live stock.

Therefore the remainder of eighty-five to ninety per cent of the western wheat crop is not used for the production of flour for domestic use in Canada. Eastern wheat is practically all used for domestic purposes in Canada. Ordinarily about 6 million to 7 million bushels is milled for flour, mostly for pastry and cake flour, the remainder of the wheat crop of eastern Canada being used as feed. Therefore the whole wheat crop of eastern Canada is generally used for domestic purposes. The amount of the western wheat crop that goes into flour in Canada, to be used by the bakers, is from five to seven and a half per cent. The proportion of flour from the western wheat crop that is sold to the housewives of Canada amounts to about the same percentage; and by far the greater part of the flour sold to the housewives of Canada is purchased and used upon the farms of this country.
The position of the farmer in the last war was that his price was held down because of a scarcity. The price of wheat in the last war cannot be used as a guide for the price of wheat in this war, but it is surely reasonable to expect that in this war the government and people of Canada should see to it that the apparent surplus of wheat is not used to depress the price of wheat in this country to an unduly low level.
There is another thing I should like to say in connection with the wheat farmers of Canada. The greatest trouble we have encountered in our whole economy, and the economy of the allies during this war, is that we found practically no one who was organized to produce the amount of material we needed for the war. Our manufacturers, our producers of other farm products than wheat, our shipbuilders-none of these could turn over to the government of this country or to the allies the required amounts of any materials required for the war. Only one person stands out in this regard in our economy; that is the wheat farmer.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS

There has been no worry whatever on the part of Great Britain or our other allies in regard to bread during this war. As I follow through, my hon. friend may see some reason. An examination of these figures shows that prices of wheat and flour bear little relationship to the price of bread. They show clearly that the flour price to the baker could be raised considerably without affecting the price of bread in Canada to-day. The figures show clearly also that with wheat prices considerably above 90 cents Fort William, flour has in the past been sold at prices per barrel Montreal and Toronto which were under present ceiling prices.
I wish to be absolutely fair to both millers and bakers of Canada. If the war-time prices and trade board maintain that present ceilings for bread and flour must be continued in order that Canadian consumers may be fairly dealt with, then wheat should be sold to the millers for the production of flour to be consumed in Canada at 90 cents a bushel Fort William until such time as the millers can prove that that is not the proper price for wheat to be milled and sold as flour under present ceiling prices. At no time should the Canadian miller pay more than can be procured elsewhere for wheat to be milled into flour. At no time should the wheat producer sell to the Canadian miller at a lower net price than can be obtained elsewhere. We must bear in mind, of course, that the war has upset our regular markets, that it is difficult to ship, but these factors should not detract too much from the value of wheat in our hands at the present time.
If it is found necessary to subsidize the Canadian miller in order to maintain the ceiling price of flour so that the Canadian consumer can be placed in a preferred position in regard to bread and flour, the responsibility

is that of the Dominion of Canada, not of the wheat producers of Canada. Before a proper price for flour to the baker can be determined, many economies in that industry will have to be effected. Wrapping, slicing and delivery could be greatly curtailed. It certainly looks like a waste to see two, three or four bread carts or trucks covering the same block in a city day after day. All these expenses enter into the cost of a loaf of bread. More people in this country could carry home their bread. There are people in a great many parts of the world who would walk quite a distance to-day to get even a part of a loaf of bread. A one-pound loaf of bread contains only about one-half pound of flour. At the present price to bakers in Canada, that one-half pound of flour is worth exactly one and a quarter cents, or about fifteen per cent of the cost of the loaf of bread. You cannot make any great economy there, you have to make it somewhere else. So, before you start to economize on the wheat or the flour that goes into the bread, you must first look at the other costs. The flour that bakers use is second patent, which is sold at a much lower cost than the first patent flour which is used by the housewife.
In connection with the milling industry, before we start to economize on wheat there are possible savings which might be surveyed in connection with packaging and methods of sale and distribution. First of all, we must determine the proper price relationship between first patent flour used by the housewife and second patent flour used by the miller, or the baker. I did not make a mistake altogether there because in many cases in this country the bakers are the millers. We must consider the price of export flour in relation to both types of flour sold in Canada, the prices of feed flour, bran, shorts and middlings; all these factors and many more must be taken into consideration before the price of wheat can be determined to maintain flour at ceiling prices.
The prices of other grains as set forth to-day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce bear a fairly proper relationship to the advance of ninety cents a bushel for wheat. Coarse grains are badly needed, and a floor of forty-five cents under oats would assure the farmer of his position in growing oats in relation to wheat. A floor of sixty cents under barley would assure the farmer of his position there and, in my opinion, would switch many farmers in the coming year from the growing of wheat to the growing of barley. A price of $2.25 a bushel for flax may appear high to some, but it will not greatly increase the production of

flax because of price alone. Flax is a speculative crop. It is difficult to produce and handle and it is of low average yield.

The western farmer is the best citizen we have in this country and wants to pull his weight during this war.
The wheat acreage reduction enunciated by the Minister of Agriculture is a common-sense policy that will tend to increase the production of badly needed coarse grains. The amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are there to protect producers of low yielding crops. The amendment made in order to allow the Minister of Agriculture to declare an emergency year regardless of price is a proper one because the farmer who will have a low yield this year has it because he has no control whatsoever over the circumstances. He will do the same job that any other farmer will do, but if climatic conditions are such that his yield will be low he should be projected and kept in a position to be ready to produce again as quickly as possible.
I still consider that a proper price for wheat in Canada is at least $1.20 a bushel, basis Fort William, in comparison with prices of other commodities in this country. I have not time at the moment to quote from a booklet I have here, but I would advise all members of the house to read it. It is put out by one of the western grain companies, and is known as the Searle Grain Index. It gives a complete picture of the western wheat grower and shows that whereas costs of living to the industrial workers have risen from 100 in 1913-14 to 146 to-day and their wages to considerably above that figure of 146, the western wheat grower whose costs were 100 in 1913-14 has costs of 150 to-day, and under the old price of wheat, 74 cents a bushel, basis Fort William, his revenue from wheat amounts to 81 per cent of what it was in 1913-14.

Along with others in this House of Commons I have endeavoured for some years to inform the Canadian people and the members of the House of Commons of the position of the western farmer in our economy:	I have tried to show them the
advisability of meting out justice and fair play to the western farmer, and we have made substantial gains in that regard both in this house and in the country. I am certain that there has been a great change in the-attitude of members from all parts of the dominion in regard to the plight of the people of western Canada and1 that to-day they are better informed and more sympathetic. Slowly but surely the members of this House of Commons and the people of Canada generally are coming to see that the present wheat surplus is not a burden but a great asset to this country.
Wheat is the most valuable food in wartime. The Secretary of Agriculture of the United States has stated that food will write the peace. It will, and food, especially wheat, will help to fight this war. The promise of food, notably wheat, to the enslaved peoples of Europe will do wonders for the allies once they start to invade Europe, and that surplus of wheat now held in our elevators in Canada can then be used to great advantage. A large part of that surplus will be badly needed by our valiant ally, Russia, in the very near future. Governments of European countries which have been overrun are to-day carrying in other parts of the world large sums of money which they can and will use for the purpose of buying wheat for their peoples just as quickly as they can be liberated. Much of that money will be used to purchase wheat from this continent as soon as that is made possible. As a matter of fact, the government of one overrun country in Europe to-day have purchased some millions of bushels of wheat and some millions of bushels of barley, and they have that wheat and barley, not as an option, but bought and paid for and stored to-day in Canada and the United States against the day when their people are liberated. Wheat is valuable and will be

Wheat Acreage Reduction

valuable. Gradually the people of Canada are coming to see that it is a short-sighted policy to gauge wheat as a burden at this time.
With these thoughts in mind, Mr. Speaker, and looking at the broad picture of agriculture in Canada to-day, taking into account the assured position of the farmer in regard to butter, milk and milk products, cheese, cattle, hogs, wool, eggs, flax, barley, and oats, and an advanced price for wheat of 90 cents a bushel, which is still too low in my estimation, and in addition the wdieat acreage reduction policy announced to-day by the Minister of Agriculture and amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, I commend both the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the information which he has given to the house and the policy he has brought down to-day, and the Minister of Agriculture, and I say to the government that on the whole they have done a good job and I am going to support them on all these measures.

Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to express to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the appreciation of myself and my constituents of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Some weeks ago I communicated with several of my constituents as to what they thought the proper wheat policy should be for this year. I did so for the reason that I believed there was too much concentration on the question of price and not enough attention paid to some of the other things which had been done by the Minister of Agriculture and this government. I got 194 replies, seventy beseeching me at all costs to see that nothing was done to detract in any way from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, that it should be left as it is, if not impro\ ed, but that payments under it might be a little more liberal. Of the others, eighty said they wanted to be sure that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was left in force, and they would like an increase in the price if it were possible for the government to grant it. Of the 194 letters which I got, 150 therefore laid their main emphasis on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Many of them said it was the first time that any government had done anything to add a certain amount of -security to the position of the farmer on our western plains, subject as he is to the continual fear of crop failure.
The situation so far as the present Minister of Agriculture is concerned has been this, as I see it: that he, coming from western Canada, knows as well as anybody living in that country the difficult position of the western farmers; but, being a member of a government which must govern with the consent of a majority of the people of Canada, naturally
IMr. J. G. Ross.]
he cannot dictate the policy of that government, and it has only been possible for him to secure the adoption of some of the ideas which he thought necessary. For that reason, because everything was not done which we in western Canada advocated and which, I believe, the minister would have liked to see done, there has been a tendency on the part of some elements to concentrate their attacks upon him and to pretend that he has not done his best for the western farmers. In my humble judgment the present Minister of Agriculture has done more for the farmers of the west than any other Minister of Agriculture since confederation. I would like those who attack him to remember that no matter what government is in power, be it Liberal, Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or Social Credit, of necessity a majority of their parliamentary supporters would come from elsewhere than western Canada, and that the west cannot hope to dictate to a dominion government, no matter of what political stripe. If we are to have fairness in public life we must give credit where credit is due.
Further, to what does this sort of campaign lead in a country like ours? The man who takes the initiative in fighting for a minority, such as are the western farmers, finds that the more he gets in the public eye, the more severely he is condemned. The result of such attacks is to create a tendency on the part of many public men to take the attitude that the less we do, the less we are in the public eye. If we are in a position such as western representatives find themselves in, the less we are in the public eye, the less likely we are to provoke attack, and therefore the best way to get by is to do as little as possible.
Another thing to be remembered is that the history of representatives from western Canada shows that time after time, after they have fought their very best to get a square deal for the west, the fact that they were not able to get all that westerners thought they should get has been the basis of charges that they had "sold out" the people and not represented them as they should have done. As a result, we have destroyed some of the best fighters for western Canada who ever came to parliament. The effect of this kind of thing is that western representatives, including those supporting a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government, if ever there is one in this country, will be advised by the cynic, "Don't fight too hard for your western farmers, because you will never satisfy them, you will not be able to get the rest of the country to agree with what you want to do, and ultimately you will be 'crucified' no matter how hard you work or what you accomplish."

Wheat Acreage Reduction
I suggest to our people in the west that they try to sort out their friends from their enemies, that they distinguish the people who are trying to serve them to the best of their ability and are getting results, even if not all they would like, from the people who pretend that if they were in office all would be like paradise as far as western Canada is concerned. I hope the people of the west will not be misled by the campaign which has been carried on, as I see it, against a man who, in the position of Minister of Agriculture, has worked harder for western Canada than any man who previously occupied that position.

When the house rose I was dealing with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and I wish to deal further with it for a few minutes before I pass on to the price of wheat.
As I understood the minister, the suggestion is made that the government is taking power to declare an emergency year even if the average price of wheat is over 80 cents, basis No. 1 northern Fort William, during the three fall months; but it is not proposed to change subsection 1 of section 2 of the act, which provides that the amount that may be paid in townships which have an average yield of eight to twelve bushels to the acre shall be paid on the basis of the average price of wheat between 70 to 80 cents. In other words, as the act now stands, if the average price during
the three fall months is, say 72 cents No. 1 northern, Fort William, the amount paid1 in townships in that category, the 8 to 12 bushel, would be 80 cents per acre on one-half the cultivated acreage. If the price were 75 cents, the price that could be allotted in the townships from 8 to 12 bushels average per acre would be 50 cents per acre. If the initial price of wheat is raised to 90 cents and if the grain exchange functions at all, I presume it will function at a price over 90 cents, so by that very fact, unless this section is amended, the people who have received assistance in the past in the 8 to 12 bushel category will not get it any more. The reason for no change being made is, I believe, that the price being raised to 90 cents, you do not need to worry very much about the person in the 8 to 12 bushel category. I do not agree, for anyone in that category, supposing he had 8 bushels per acre, would have only six bushels for sale, and that would mean he would not have very much income.
I suggest that very serious consideration should be given to amending this so that in an emergency year anyone in the 8 to 12 bushel category should get a dollar just the same as anyone in the 4 to 8 bushel category would get S1.50 for half his cultivated acreage.
Some may think that would mean a tremendous drain on the treasury. I took the trouble to look up the relative amounts paid in the various categories in the last two years, namely, 1939-40 and 1940-41. The year 1941-42 is not yet complete, so I have not those figures.

That meant actually a subsidizing of the price of wheat by the treasury of this country to the extent of a little over one cent a bushel.
