ating almost half of the money paid out under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
I submit that in view of the fact that this policy cost the treasury of this country only a little over one cent a bushel (spread over all wheat marketed) and that it means so much in the way of security to the'western farmer, and has cost the treasury in two years only a little over eleven and a half million dollars, when you are increasing the price to the farmer who has wheat you should not deprive the farmer who has a small crop of eight to twelve bushels of the bit of protection he has already.
I most earnestly urge the government to make an amendment so that you do not take away from the farmer in the eight to twelve category the bit of protection he has under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
The benefit received under this act in the case of crop failure is $2.50 per acre; on half your acreage that is $1.25 an acre. Anyone who knows anything about farming in western Canada knows that is not adequate for a farmer to pay for his loss of crop and keep himself and family during the next year.
Instead of cutting down the payment I earnestly suggest that the government consider increasing the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and particularly in that category, and that the protection now given in the eight to twelve category should not be taken away.
Coming now to the question of the price of wheat, I should like to urge this House of Commons to approach the matter of dealing with our western Canadian farmer in the same spirit as that in which we asked our people to approach the problem of dealing with people in other countries. We know that last August the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Right Hon. Winston Churchill, and the President of the United States, met and signed what is known as the Atlantic charter, Clause 6 of that charter reads:
After the final destruction of the nazi tyranny they hope to see established a peace which will afford to all nations the means of dwelling in safety within their own boundaries, and which will afford assurance that all the men in all the lands may live out their lives in freedom from fear and want.
Mr. Speaker, if that is the objective for which we are fighting this war, that the people in all lands of the world should be able to live out their lives in freedom from fear and want, is it not time that the members of this house should actually say that they will apply that to their own fellow Canadians? Continually I am meeting fellow Canadians in western Canada who say, "Here are the noble principles of the Atlantic charter;

Canadians in western Canada are sending their men in as large a proportion as any other part of Canada to fight for these principles; if we cannot get them at home, what real hope is there of getting them established in the world at large?"
Some one may say that I am exaggerating the situation. I have not much time to prove my point, but I think I can give some figures that will establish it to any fair-minded man in this house.
The province of Saskatchewan made a submission to the Sirois commission, and in that connection they made a very careful survey of their debt situation. They found that the agricultural debt in Saskatchewan in 1937 was $525,000,000. I need not go into the reason for that, except to say that no doubt the interest being charged was too high. Many people were paying more than eight per cent. If the interest had been five per cent and the debts had been amortized, there would have been very little debt comparatively in western Canada in 1937. But be that as it may, the debt upon Saskatchewan farming was $525,000,000, or $15 for every acre of cultivated land in that province.
Everyone knows also that during the past several years, with prices so low, certainly the farmer needed the two-thirds of the crop he was allowed to retain to live on and the one-third left would often barely pay taxes and perhaps a very little on the principal and interest. What has been the situation, then? I wish this to be considered by people in the other parts of Canada. Year after year men who went into that country in the early days, who worked there during all their lives and had their families working with them, who lived on a very low standard of living, have seen their equity being cut down, until finally someone has come along and said, "You no longer have any equity left in your land." Then what happens? When they get around seventy years of age they are told, "You might as well let us foreclose, and you can live on the old age pension," or something to that effect. I venture to say that seventy-five per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan have seen their equities in their land and their homes gradually disappear. The farmer has no place to go with his family, unless he wishes to go on relief in the cities and towns. He sees his equity vanishing; he sees the time approaching when he will be told that his equity is gone and that he might as well let himself be foreclosed. Could anyone in this house say that those farmers, seeing their equity reduced inexorably year after year, were free from fear, the fear of losing their homes and, with their families, being cast out? I know it will be said that there is

debt adjustment legislation which is intended to prevent these foreclosures; but when the equity is wiped out, the tendency is for the man to be told, "You no longer have an equity, and you might as well quit struggling."
This is something we should all consider. I absolutely agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that if we are not well on the way to a new order in Canada before this war ends, then our chances of getting it after the war are not so good. I ask the government, as I ask every hon. member, in approaching this question of the price of wheat to bear in mind the situation which prevails in western Canada, and to determine that we in this house will apply the principles of the Atlantic charter to our fellow Canadians. '
As an example of what is happening, not only on western farms but all over Canada, in the 1941 "Canada Year Book" I find that the average value of farms and equipment in Canada in 1941 is given as 813,814. For 1931 it is given as $7,185, a drop of over $6,000 for the average Canadian farm and equipment, or almost fifty per cent. If you have operating also an increase in debt due to inability to pay 'interest and principal, you can see how equities can be reduced year by year. Someone may say, "Well, your western farmer lives too extravagantly." Again I go to the year book; I cannot give all the figures, but I should like to compare the western farmer with the Ontario farmer in certain respects. I find that according to the census of 1931 Ontario farmers having cars comprised 65-4 per cent of the farmers of Ontario, while the farmers of Saskatchewan having cars comprised only 47-7 per cent. Ontario farmers with telephones comprised 54-1 per cent; in Saskatchewan the figure was 34-2 per cent. In Ontario 21-5 per cent of the farmers had radios; in Saskatchewan 20-2 per cent had radios. Ontario farmers having gas or electricity totalled 16-8 per cent, while in Saskatchewan the figure was 2-S per cent. Farmers having piped water in their kitchens, and so on, totalled 10-4 per cent in Ontario and only 1-4 per cent in Saskatchewan.
This situation is reflected in our educational services, our medical services and all the other services we give our people. To-day it is extremely difficult to get doctors to stay in rural districts; it is very difficult to keep rural schools open in more outlying districts particularly. Here is the situation, and I put it to members of this house point blank. Would you, for any reason, I do not care what it is, say you are going to have one first-class type of citizen in Canada and then another, a second-class type, who cannot afford the same education, who cannot afford the same medical services as people in other parts of the
country, at the same time that you are asking these young men to go out and give their lives, together with the first-class citizens of Canada? These may be regarded as harsh words. We can close our ears to them if we wish, but the facts are there, for every member of this house to see. We are all members of the Canadian parliament, and we should not close our eyes to the situation that is before us.
Someone may say, "Well, you have not proved that your income is low in Saskatchewan." I should like to give a great many figures, but I might give just enough to indicate that there is real truth in what I am saying. I have before me figures as to the per capita national income by provinces in 1927 and 1940; I have them for all the provinces, but I cannot take time to give all those figures. The average per capita income in Ontario in 1927 is $511. In Saskatchewan, in the same year, the average per capita income was $466. Then we come to 1940. In that year the average per capita national income in Ontario had dropped to $505, but in Saskatchewan it dropped to $261, or by almost fifty per cent. Then we might take the receipts from the sale of farm products, by provinces, which will give the gross agricultural income, based on the average from 1926 to 1929. In Quebec the average income during that period was $101,000,000, in round figures. In 1941 that income had increased to $136,000,000. The average agricultural income in Ontario from 1926 to 1929 was $260,000,000, and in 1941 it had increased to $284,000,000. In other words, there was an increase in both Ontario and Quebec in the gross agricultural income. What was the situation in Saskatchewan? The average income from 1926 to 1929 was $280,000,000, but in 1941 that income shrank to $156,000,000. I ask any hon. members representing Ontario and Quebec just what their farmers would do to them if the agricultural income of their provinces, instead of going up, had shrunk by almost half; and I ask hon. members representing eastern farming communities, who may oppose some measure of justice for the western farmer, what they would do if they were in our position.
Then I might quote some figures as to the index number of receipts from the sale of farm products, using the period 1926 to 1929 as 100. In Quebec the index number in 1941 was 134-6; in Ontario it was 109-3; in Saskatchewan, 55-9, and in Manitoba, 98-1. After all, Saskatchewan is the province that suffers most in the present situation because in 1940, for example, 76 per cent of our total agricultural income was derived from wheat, while in 1941, 71 per cent of our income came from wheat which is most depressed in price of any agricultural product. I would speak to the

labouring people of this country-and I am glad the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is interested. No farmer objects to labour being well treated, but we ask labour to have some sympathy for us when we ask for a fair deal, too.
I have before me a report of the Searle Grain Company, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). I am going to read only two paragraphs from it:
Looking at the two charts-
It gives a chart showing camparative receipts of labour and farmers.
-it will be observed that for wheat to have the same purchasing power as it had in 1913 and 1914, . . . the price should now be one dollar. This is at the average country point. . . .
In other words, the parity price for wheat, if it is to have the same purchasing power as it did in 1913 and 1914, should be one dollar to the farmer-and that means $1.20 a bushel at Fort William. That would put the farmer in the same position as he occupied back in 1913 and 1914-not the good old days between 1926 and 1929. He has reached a point where he is almost 50 per cent worse off than he was in 1913.
We now turn to the industrial worker. This is where I say he should give some support to the position taken by the farmers. The industrial worker's average hourly wage, if it is to have the same purchasing power as it did in 1913 and 1914, should now stand at the index number of 145. In other words, where the industrial labour got $100 in 1913, to purchase the same amount of goods to-day he should get $145. What is he getting? He is actually getting $210. In other words, the industrial worker to-day is better off by 44 per cent than he was in 1913-1914, and the farmer is roughly 45 per cent worse off-that is wheat at the price prevailing last year.
The suggestion was made that we should freeze the farmer in that inferior position. At a time when the industrial labourer would be getting only $145 compared with $100 in 191314, to be as well off, and when in fact he is actually receiving $210, the suggestion is that the farmer should get only $54 where he got $100, and that his position should: be frozen there. Is it any wonder that the hon. member for Moose Jaw and every other western farmer says that we refuse to be placed1 in that position of inferiority compared with the rest of Canada? Is it any wonder that the west takes that attitude? We have children to look after and to educate; we have medical services to obtain; we are human beings, just the same as the industrial workers.
Mark this: whereas the total average income per farm in 1926-29 was $1,007 a year, the aver-

age yearly earning of industrial workers was $1,017, or roughly $10 more a year. That was the condition, in spite of the fact that the farmer has an investment in his land. During the period 1930-40 that had shrunk to an average income per farmer of $468 a year, while that of the industrial worker was $902. During that time the average investment in farms was $7,185, and the average income per farm during the same ten years had fallen from $1,007 to $468.
In spite of the investment involved, and in spite of the fact that that is total farm income, for, let us remember, the farmer works, his wife works and his children work. It seems to me that the time has come when everybody in Canada should know those figures, and act according to the principle laid down in the Atlantic charter. We should act, as well as talk in that regard.
What objections are made? One objection is that there is too much wheat. I believe the hon. member for Moose Jaw dealt thoroughly with this point this afternoon. Let me read what Mr. Churchill had to say:
We shall do our best to encourage the building up of reserves of food all over the world, so that there will always be held before the eyes of the people of Europe, including the Germans, the certainty that the shattering of nazi power would bring them all immediate food, freedom and peace.
In other words, one of the weapons for the destruction of nazi tyranny is the tremendous over-supply of wheat we have built up in Canada. Mr. Churchill says that we will encourage that. Are we encouraging it when we say that we will pay less than the cost of production for that wheat, just because the farmer is doing the very thing that Mr. Churchill, that incomparable leader of democracy, has said we will do? That is all I shall have to say on the suggestion that we have too much wheat. But the day will come when every bushel of wheat will feed some hungry mouth that will be very happy to receive it.
It is suggested that we should go into other lines of production. Well, I shall not take time to give figures, but I might point out in passing that Saskatchewan hog marketing increased from 312,000 head in 1939 to 857,000 head in 1941. That is an increase of well over 200 per cent, and if she went on increasing at the same rate during the next two years she would produce as many hogs as Ontario does now.
For those who say that we should turn our entire effort to the production of mixed products, I have some interesting figures. Assuming that to-day we can use 230,000,000 bushels of wheat, that our average crop would be 450,000,000 bushels, and that we turned the remaining 220,000,000 bushels to the production of hog products, we would produce in hogs alone 2,640,000,000 pounds. Yes, think

of it-2,640,000,000 pounds! Our entire marketings last year amounted to only 1,245,000,000 pounds of hog products. In other words, if we turned our entire excess wheat production to the feeding of hogs, we would produce in Saskatchewan alone more than twice the total amount of hogs marketed in all of Canada. I say to hon. members from Ontario: Supposing you drive the Saskatchewan farmer to do that, in what position will it leave your constituents when we in Saskatchewan produce twice as much as the whole of Canada combined? That is a point which must be faced,

An hon. member says,
"Don't worry about us, we shall be all right." Well, I am glad he is so optimistic. But I suggest that the path of true statesmanship is not to shove your head in the sand and say, "We shall be all right."
There is the further suggestion that wheat is no advantage to Canada. Between the years 1910 and 1936 the value of grain marketed from western Canada alone was $10,278,000,000. That went to build up eastern Canada, as no other single factor has built it up. In the days ahead, when we get out of this period of interference with markets, western Canada once more will make a vital contribution to the upbuilding of the rest of Canada. Do not drive that country, which has done so much to build up Canada as a whole, away from the industry it has developed.
Then the suggestion is made that we should swing over to manufacturing. I have something to say in that regard which is aside from the subject. Hon. members will perhaps bear with me for a moment, or maybe permit me to have a minute or two extra to deal with it. There are 20,000,000,000 tons of coal in Estevan, perhaps one of the largest deposits of soft coal in the world. I suggest to the government: if you are having a total war effort, why do you not develop a tremendous head of power at the Estevan mine and have the advantage of all the by-products that would be obtained? Some of those by-products I believe could be used to make synthetic rubber. Probably a half-million people could be put to work in industry as a result who now have no chance to participate in the war effort.
I grant that it might cost a little more to manufacture in western Canada, but while a tank that costs fifty per cent more to make may do something to the national debt of this country; it will kill a nazi just the same as a tank manufactured more cheaply in eastern Canada. We have not a total war effort when the prairie provinces have only a few hundred thousand dollars worth of munition contracts. All we in Saskatchewan have been
permitted to do in the war is to send our young men to enlist or our young men and women to the coast or down to eastern Canada to work. But some of them cannot leave home and they would be very glad to engage in industry. I know the answer will be that we have not the management.

We can ship steel out to the west just the same as we can ship it to the east. Surely we can get it. After all, if we are not going to lay the foundation for stepping up our production to a one hundred per cent effort, then we are not doing our part toward'the people of this country. I ask my hon. friend who has just interrupted me: Does he think that because it cost extra money to establish industries behind the Ural mountains, Russia hesitated to do it when the very life of that country was at stake? Did they consider the question of money and the cost of doing these things? I ask the government, which I am proud and pleased to follow, in this time of world crisis, to do the thing that is necessary to mobilize this country's industrial capacity one hundred per cent.
On the question of management, we know that we had not the management at the outbreak of this war, for example, to provide an armoured division for Canada. You have to train management in industry the same as you are training men for an armoured division or in the commonwealth air training scheme. Once you have trained your management in eastern Canada, can it not be moved in part out west to establish industries there alongside these tremendous coal fields? Some people who may feel that they are wiser than I, and properly so, will say that this is going to cost more money, that it will be difficult and so on. I say that it might be the last ounce of strength put into the effort that will win this war. Many of us at one time or another have had our car stuck. We have tried to get it out and have almost succeeded. If a little child had come along and put his shoulder to the car, it would have come out, but for the lack of that extra few pounds pressure, the car rolled back into the hole and it probably finally required a tractor to pull it out.
The same situation exists so far as our position in this war is concerned. Anyone who is a soldier knows that when the battle trembles in the balance, one man thrown into the fray might turn the tide. I think Canada should make up her mind to put her whole strength into this war. She should make sure that western Canada is given a chance to do what it can do as well as any other part of the country. If you say to western Canada, "turn to other things," we will reply that we will turn to other things if you will only give us a chance to do so.

I have exceeded my time by two or three minutes, and I shall not impose upon the goodwill of the house more than to say a few words in conclusion. In my opinion -the proper price for wheat when compared with other things would be $1.20 a bushel, basis Fort William. To pay that price would cost $75,000,000 -a year. For three years, the total cost would be $225,000,000. Would it make much difference three years from now whether the debt of this country was, say $10,200,000,000 or $10,425,000,000? The people of western Canada are in this war just the same as any other Canadians, but they see farmers across the line in the United States getting 10 per cent over parity prices for -their wheat. They ask whether they are not fighting just the same as those people across the line. I suggest to the government that it would be a good thing for the unity of this country if we treated our western farmers just as well as the United States treat their western farmers. I suggest that the actual cost to the taxpayers of this county would be nil because that debt will be renewed from time to time. A difference of $225,000,000 in a debt of the size it will be at the end of the war will not make much difference to the Minister of Finance of that day.
But the difference in the attitude of the people of western Canada, their ability to support the war and their feeling that they are felt, by the rest of Canada to be a real part of this country will be tremendous. I appeal to the government to bear in mind the fact that these loyal, honest, hard-working people are one with you in the great fight which we face. I ask you to treat them as first-class citizens, as fellow' Canadians, as brothers in arms-do not treat them as second-class citizens-and the result will be tenfold in the response that you will get, in the strength that you will get as we all get together as a united people to fight the battles that lie ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I withdraw it. I was just having a little joke and I think, if we had a few little jokes of that kind instead of the kind more often practised in this house, we would have a much healthier atmosphere here. But what I have to say with regard to the agricultural policy I do not intend to apologize for or to withdraw.
The agricultural policy of this country for a number of years has been very truly described by the hon. gentleman who got so warm at my statement just now and insisted upon my withdrawing it. I think he made a very good case for the farmers of western Canada and Canadians generally, because in putting up the case for the western farmer I realize, as must every other hon. member, that a case is being put up for all of Canada. We cannot have poor relations in this country, as agriculture might well be described, if we are to have that Canadian unity which has been shouted about so loud and so long in this house.
As they gave us their policies for agriculture this afternoon I was wondering just who were the advisers of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), and I wondered because agriculture is not getting the same treatment as other classes in Canada. I attended a banquet at the Chateau Laurier not very long ago, on January 29, I believe, when we had the pleasure and profit of listening to Mr. R. M. Evans, Administrator of Agricultural Adjustment and Conservation, United! States Department of Agriculture. I was very glad to hear this gentleman who had been invited to Canada, and I was also very glad to see sitting on the platform with him the Minister of Agriculture. I have the speech of Mr. Evans here, and while I shall not read all of it, I should like to quote a few paragraphs from his address because I think they are well worth noting. He said:
It is all very well to talk about men being free in a democracy-for in a true democracy, they are. But it is only a matter of being realistic-for the protection of democracy itself -to recognize that when farmers who produce the food that a nation needs must sell their products at low prices, over which they have no control, and then lose their farms, their homes, and family security because they cannot meet their obligations-then those men are not truly free. They do not have economic freedom, and without it political freedom cannot long endure. Democracy needs bread and butter as well as ballots.
At the present time, when our young men and our young women are overseas fighting for democracy, I think it is only right that we should practise that same democracy here at home. A little further along Mr. Evans had this to say in connection with reserves:
To carry these reserves, as well as to smooth out the flow of crops to market, commodity loans are made to producers who have complied with their acreage allotments. These loans are based upon 85 per cent of the parity price for the commodity. For wheat, this has meant a loan rate of $1.15 per bushel for No. 2 hard winter at Chicago this year. At this price, the wheat in an average loaf of bread costs about one and three-quarters cents. The fact that wheat for some time now has been above the loan rate would seem to indicate that our farmers have succeeded in making it their market.
Under normal circumstances, this system of marketing appears to be adequate. But when the surplus of any basic commodity reaches a danger point, the law requires that a marketing quota be declared. The quota must be approved by two-thirds of the affected producers voting in a referendum.
I may point out that in this country the producers have not one thing to say about quotas. Instead, a policy of totalitarianism is practised. Mr. Evans went on to say:
Rounding out this programme of protection for the producer is crop insurance against losses from natural, unavoidable hazards. It insures yield only, not price. Crop insurance was provided on wheat for the first time in 1939 and is being extended to cotton this year.
In concluding my references to Mr. Evans'' address, I should like to summarize the six points of the United States farm programme, as follows:
1.	Conservation based upon sound soil improving crops and practices with payment in proportion to the work accomplished.
2.	Acreage allotments to adjust production to need-with payments for adjustment and to improve income.
3.	Marketing loans with farm storage allowances.
4.	Marketing quotas when supplies hit danger levels.
5.	Crop insurance-now offered on cotton and wheat.
6.	Market expansion programme including school lunches, food stamp plan and direct distribution to low income groups as well as export assistance when necessary.
A little further on he says:
During November, AAA farmer committeemen visited every one of their six million neighbours to sign them up in the AAA farm programme for 1942. Each farmer prepared a farm plan and indicated how much of each crop or product he intended to produce next year. The reports now show that our farmers intend to meet or exceed the goals we have set for the production of "food for freedom" in 1942.

Wheat Acreage Reduction

Just one other quotation from his address:
In every county and community, our programme is run by farmer committeemen elected by their neighbours. From the ranks of these 130,000 committeemen, our state committees are appointed by the secretary of agriculture. Many of the men in administrative, policyforming positions in our Department of Agriculture are farmers who have come up through the ranks of our farm programme in these past eight or nine years.
I have pleasure in commending this address of Mr. Evans to the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues in the government. Following that up, I should like to read a section of the statute which has been passed by congress dealing with parity prices. Section 3 (a) of the price control bill which became law in the United States on January 30 last states:
Sec. 3 (a) No maximum price shall be established or maintained for any agricultural commodity below the highest of any of the following prices, as determined and published by the Secretary of Agriculture: (1) 110 per centum of the parity price for such commodity, adjusted by the Secretary of Agriculture for grade, location, and seasonal differentials, or. in case a comparable price has been determined for such commodity under subsection (b), 110 per centum of such comparable price, adjusted in the same manner, in lieu of 110 per centum of the parity price so adjusted; (2) the market price prevailing for such commodity on October 1, 1941; (3) the market price prevailing for such commodity on December 15, 1941; or (4) the average price for such commodity during the period July 1, 1919, to June 30, 1929.
I believe that in this respect we should follow the action of the United States-because we always seem to wait for somebody else to take the lead, and then we follow. The United States has given us a very good lead in this case, and I commend it to the Minister of Agriculture and the government.
From time to time delegations representing the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and similar bodies have come to Ottawa. One of the last to appear here were the 400 or so representatives from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. This delegation was organized, I believe, by the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and included, as well as the Saskatchewan delegation, representatives of Manitoba farm and other organizations, the United Farmers of Alberta, the United Farmers of Canada, Alberta section, and the Alberta wheat pool. When the representatives of these bodies met the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and some members of his cabinet they were, I understand, very favourably received. They were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) that their demands were just and reasonable, and none other than the Prime Minister himself told the delegation, according to press reports, that the wheat question was one wdth which Canada should 
deal, that it was Canada's responsibility. Now we are asking that Canada shoulder this responsibility. Some seem to think that we are too persistent in pressing this matter, but I believe that those who express this opinion do not really understand the situation in the west, as it has been so well described by the hon. member who preceded me. I have here a little poem which originated in North Dakota. It reads as follows:
I hate to be a kicker, I always long for peace,
But the wheel that does the squeaking is the one that gets the grease.
It's nice to be a peaceful soul, and not too hard to please,
But the dog that's always scratching is the one that has the fleas.
The art of soft soap spreading is the thing that palls and stales,
But the guy who wields the hammer is the one who drives the nails.
Let us not put any notions that are harmful in your head,
But the baby that keeps yelling is the baby that gets fed!

speechtext:
A great many "babies" have
been crying in Canada, and a whole lot of them must have been fed, because we do not hear them crying any more. So, now that everybody else has been satisfied, perhaps Canada will see to it that the farmer receives a little of what is coming to him.
I have here a publication which was put out by the Searle Grain company, of Winnipeg, dealing with prices and amounts which have been received by the farmers. I will read the following extract:
During the past eleven crop years our farmers have delivered to market 3,084 million bushels of grain. They have received for this in cash 1,709 million dollars. Had all these bushels of wheat enjoyed the same purchasing power as a bushel of wheat did in 1913-14 or been at so-called "parity" level-and no one considers wheat had too great a purchasing power in 1913-14-our farmers would have been able to pay for additional goods, commodities, services, debts and so forth to the additional value of 1,127 million dollars.
That is the amount which has been legally stolen from our western farmers; it is money which they would have received if they were getting the treatment to which they were entitled:
. . . our farmers would have been able to pay for additional goods, commodities, services, debts and so forth to the additional value of 1,127 million dollars.
That sum, I believe, would have supplied a whole lot of milk and have satisfied a great many "babies" and kept them from crying.

Wheat Acreage Reduction
Had any other class or group in Canada been deprived of any such amount as that, I believe you would have had, as we had in 1939, a sit-down strike. I am referring to what industry threatened when profits were restricted to five per cent. But we farmers have continued ever since 1929 to produce below cost of production and we have not yet gone on a sit-down strike. So I believe we are loyal citizens; we have been just a little too "easy" for our own good; we should get the consideration now which all those other "babies" have received who have now been satisfied.
According to other information contained in this booklet, Canadian wheat, to be at the 1913-14 parity, would require a price of about $1.20 for No. 1 northern in store Fort AVilliam. "To-day"-this book was written last fall- "No. 1 northern Fort William is 72f cents a bushel". In the United States, for wheat to be at the 1913-14 parity, it would require a price of approximate^ SI.22 in store Chicago. At that time May wheat, Chicago, was actually $1.19 a bushel. I think you will notice that United States wheat, although not as good as ours, has been approximately 50 cents higher for quite a long time.
The same booklet, dealing with wheat growers and industrial labour, has this to say:
The average hourly rates of industrial wages, as set out by the Department of Labour for 1940, were twice as high as, actually 104 per cent higher than, in 1913-14, and in 1941 wages have been raised still further, and in addition industrial labour has received substantial "costs of living" bonuses.
Some say that it is not fair for the government to give assistance to our wheat growers. With all courtesy, however, we draw attention to the fact that all the high wages and cost of living bonuses given to industrial workers who work directly and indirectly on war production, are themselves paid for by the government, for the government itself buys and pays for all the products of these workers.
I am not complaining about this being received by labour in industry in Canada to-day. Neither am 1 complaining of the cost of living bonus that is being paid. I have, however, a complaint that that cost of living bonus is not extended far enough. For instance, helpers in stores where only a few are employed, or in other industries where only a few are employed, khould also have the cost of living bonus.
I understand that at the present time an arrangement between Canada and the United Si^tes provides for quite an easement of tariff restrictions as far as war material is concerned. I wonder why the same could not apply to farm implements, both now and for a n umber of years past. We have not heard very much about tariffs for quite a while, and some of the "crying babies" of the past have not said anything about it either. For the 44561-74}
information of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) who has not been very long in 'his position I shall give a few figures, and I hope he takes them into consideration. I am sorry this table is not up to date, but it is the best we have been able to get. It relates to tariffs in the only year in which I know they were investigated, namely, 1931. I might say that 1931 was one of the years when we had poor crops and very poor prices, so that if a normal year were taken the various costs would be higher than I am about to quote.
In 1931 Manitoba paid by way of tariffs $29,185,40, or $13.25 per capita. In the same year Saskatchewan paid $29,228,285, or $28.16 per capita. Alberta paid $27,909,396, or $26.93 per capita. British Columbia paid $37,737,247, or $22.33 per capita.
That is to say, in that one year alone it cost the four western provinces $124,060,668 by way of tariffs, which amount would pay a great part of the wheat subsidies that we have been given in the past and should shut off a great deal of the criticism that has been offered.
Let me give some figures regarding the part of the country from which much of the criticism has been coming. The province of Quebec, as far as tariffs are concerned, had a gain of $31,685,885, which is equal to $11.03 per capita. That wonderful milch cow, Ontario, which western Canada has been feeding for the last number of years, had a gain of $51,989,761, equal to $15.15 per capita.
Perhaps that is enough; the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been listening patiently, and I hope he gets these figures and takes them into consideration in dealing further with our initial price of wheat.
A number of arguments are put up against raising the price of wheat. During the period 1926-1941 we had an average of 14-3 bushels per acre. For the years 1926-1929 the average was 18-4 bushels per acre.
The average price per bushel for 1926-1941 was 671 cents. The average price for 19261929, on which period labour wages are based, was 96J cents, or 29 cents higher than the average for 1926-1941.
The value per acre 1926-1941 was $9.65, whereas the figure for 1926-1929 inclusive was $17.44, or a drop in value per acre of $7.79.
The purchasing power index for 1926-1941 was 59 per cent, whereas the purchasing power index for 1926-1929 was 84 per cent, or a drop of 25 per cent for the 1926-1941 period.
I have here some other figures which, with the consent of the house, I should like to have placed on Hansard.

speechtext:
1910-19^1
YIELD PER ACRE	PRICE PER BUSHEL

Wheat Acreage Reduction
In 1939 the three prairie provinces received for their grain crops §264,145,000. In 1940 we received $278,770,000. In 1941 the year in which the Minister of Agriculture told us we received over 90 cents a bushel, we received $141,680,000.
The people should not be led astray and made to believe that farmers in Canada all received over 90 cents a bushel. As a practical farmer myself, the wheat which I have sold to date has netted me 48i cents a bushel, and I have not received one cent of bonus since the bonus s}'stem was introduced in 1939.
You are not an average farmer.

Well, I do my best; I try to be.
Mr. MacIvINNON (Edmonton West): You are better than the average.
I am still holding the farm, which a number of others have not been able to do.
The income from wheat was $210,000,000.

Well, the minister is trying to make an argument, and for his benefit and the benefit of the house I might point out that if one man gets 48-J cents a bushel for his wheat and another gets $1.25, which is possible under the bonus system provided he has a small enough yield, it does not mean that the average farmer gets 90 cents or over. The people should not be misled, because the farmers who are getting a wheat crop do not get the benefit of the bonus.

If the hon. member will permit, if all the farmers in western Canada got $200,000,000 on account of wheat and there were less than 200,000,000 bushels, the average amount received was more than $1 a bushel.

That is all very well, but as I said, it does not average up. The man who benefits by the prairie farm assistance bonus does not benefit by the high price of wheat, because in order to qualify for the bonus, the crop in his township must be below twelve bushels per acre. On the other hand, the man who gets a large yield, above twelve bushels to the acre, cannot benefit either. So we have two distinct problems to deal with, a higher price for wheat for the farmer who gets a crop, and a better bonus system for the farmer who does not. Averaging up and calling everyone satisfied does not work, and some change must be made before you can have a satisfactory and prosperous agriculture.
We have had a number of organizations pressing recently for a better price for wheat. First, the Saskatchewan delegation that came
here asked for an initial price of $1, and final settlement *o be made on parity price basis. I am quite satisfied with that, but the group with which I am associated and I myself have consistently advocated not less than 95 cents a bushel, and this past year or two, since the war, when costs of production have increased, we have consistently argued for and demanded $1 a bushel at the local elevator in order that farmers may live.
The Saskatchewan delegation wanted $1. with the balance to be settled as I have already mentioned. The Searle Grain Company believes that $1.20 is the parity price for wheat, while the Northwest Line Elevators set their figure at S1.22J. I do not know how anyone can expect to put up an argument that will stand analysis, to make us believe that we can grow wheat at less than $1 a bushel and hold our farms and homes. In my opinion, after close to thirty years of experience in that line of work, it cannot be done.
Perhaps someone may think we are paying our farm help too much. The average farm wage, from 1926 to 1941 inclusive, was $26.90 a month, for all of Canada. During this period the lowest wages were paid in 1933, when they averaged only $10 a month, or less than some of our "crying babies" receive as living allowance for one day, and the average in 1941 was $29.42 a month. The average during the whole period for wages and board was $46.75 a month; the lowest figure was in 1933, when it was $20, and the average for 1941 was $46.58. Then we are faced with the further problem that farmers' sons are taken off the land for the army, even though only one son is left on the farm. In many cases the farmer is too old to operate the power machinery he has bought recently, and under our present set-up the only son may be taken from the farm and put in the army. I do not for a moment say that farmers' sons should not serve. I think if an analysis could be made of all enlistments it would be found that the farmers have contributed a higher percentage than any other group in Canada; but in the interests of agriculture, in the interests of Canada and of the united nations I say that a boy who is the only help left on a farm should be allowed to stay there, because he is just as much a key man as any man in industry.
Then the minister told us that we would receive 90 cents a bushel for wheat. The average price per bushel at Fort William from 1926 to 1929 was $1.35. That was not the highest price paid during that period, but the average. For oats we are to receive 45 cents for the 1942 crop. The average for
Wheat Acreage Reduction

1926 to 1929 was 60 cents, or 15 cents more than the price offered this year. For barley we are to receive 60 cents a bushel, while the average price for 1926 to 1929 was 71.6 cents, and during that period we had fairly normal times in Canada. Then we are offered $2.25 for flax as against an average of $2.08 from 1926 to 1929. If I understood the minister aright, we cannot be paid any more because if the farmers were given the prices to which they are entitled we would not have enough money left with which to prosecute the war successfully. The minister told us that last year' we lost not less than $100,000,000 because of the price that was set. I do not think he made that amount nearly large enough.

We dropped that on
wheat, but we got some of it back from other sources.
I do not think the minister's addition was very good when he went to school, because $100,000,000 was not nearly enough.
It does not matter what it was when I went to school; it is all right now.

I do not think it has improved, considering the company he has kept since he left school. Some hon. gentlemen around me say that the minister is a magician. If I should read some of the letters I have received I do not think he would feel very much like a magician or a wizard.

I can read you mine,
too.

Little men usually have a pretty big opinion of themselves, but they do not always stack up. Then, Mr. Speaker, I said I had not received a bonus yet, and in that connection I should like to read a letter I received only a couple of days ago:
I am writing you in regards to the summer-fallow bonus. I think that it is a crime the trouble E. L. Gray is putting the farmers to, to get their bonus.
I am not blaming Mr. E. L. Gray entirely; I am just reading this letter to give hon. members an idea of how some of the farmers feel, and I do not say that Mr. Gray is responsible for all the trouble.
Myself, I have made five trips to the municipal office and each trip is thirty miles, and one to Edmonton, and still I am waiting for my bonuses, and there is quite a lot in this district that are still waiting for theirs, and I was told yesterday that we would have to go to Vermilion on February 24 and meet an inspector if we wanted our bonus. Now we have not been notified about this as they only
(Mr. Fair.]
wrote to the secretary, and I only heard it last night by a neighbour who has not got one dollar yet.
Now, Bob, you know that a lot of us in this district had almost a total crop failure, and yet a lot of us have not received a dollar bonus yet, although we are supposed to get three of them, and here it is the end of February. How in the world do they expect people to try and help in a war effort and buy victory bonds and then treat us like this?
This man must be saving, because I notice he has written on both sides of his stationery, which is not done by a number of others throughout the country. Then he goes on:
I had less than 750 bushels of wheat from 160 acres and no coarse grains on 200 acres, and yet I had about $600 in wages and $300 taxes to pay as well as my living and operating expenses.
The secretary also told me that a farmer with fifty head of cattle would not get the 75 cents cost of living bonus, yet there is a lot of farmers that have sold as high as 500 pigs who do get it. I wonder where the difference is, and the man raising cattle has been doing so at a loss for about eight years, and most farmers have only increased their cattle the last year.
That is a sample of the letters we are getting in connection with the bonuses. I have taken up a number of cases and have practically all of them cleared up after a little time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my time is almost gone-
That's good.

There are some people in this house who have not yet made a speech. Some folks call them laughing hyenas, I believe though I do not know what a laughing hyena looks like. I think it would pay these hon. gentlemen to sit quietly and keep their seats warm, because they are not doing any good anyway. They simply display a lack of the education they should have received at their mother's knee.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest' that we consider the following points, which are the policies of the group with which I am associated. The first is international cooperation between the four exporting countries, the United States, Australia, Argentina and Canada. This has been worked upon for some time, and I do not know what were the final results at Washington. I believe that would be much better than the competitive system which we have followed in the past.
Then there should be parity prices established for all agricultural products. I am not asking for any unreasonable profits, but certainly there is no reason why one class should produce below cost of production and stand

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
all the loss. We are willing to produce, and to do everything else to win the war, but in doing so there is no reason why we should run the risk of losing our farms, our homes and our morale.
I believe we should have loans on grain, as well as storage. I believe the storage could be reduced, because when we come to figure the cost of elevators, and what they bring in by way of storage charges, there is no doubt that that amount can be reduced considerably.
I believe in a policy of quotas, when necessary, because we cannot expect the government to take over all the wheat we may grow. I do not believe, however, that the growing of wheat shoidd be restricted to so great an extent, because it may be needed in the very near future.
Then, I believe that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be amended in three or four different ways. These points I shall discuss in greater detail when we are in committee of the whole. If that act were administered by local committees, in the same way that some agricultural policies are being administered in the United States, I believe we would have far better protection. I believe the township basis, on which we are now operating, is too large and that it should be on an individual basis. If we had local committees administering the act, the individual farmers would be compelled to do a far better job for themselves, and for the country as well. The limit of three thousand bushels and the live stock restriction under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be removed.
The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

I was interrupted on several occasions, and with the consent of the house I should like to have two or three more
minutes.
Go ahead.

If it is agreed, the hon. member may proceed. I would point out, however, that we are beginning to do in this debate something which I called to the attention of hon. members in an earlier debate. The forty-minute rule should not be disregarded, even with the consent of the house.

I should also like to see the grain exchange at Winnipeg closed not only for the duration of the war, but for good. As I have pointed out on several occasions, right after the war broke out the exchange in England was closed. I notice that the Argentine republic passed a decree on November 14 of last year by which they closed their grain
exchange, too. Now that we have others leading, perhaps we can follow the way, and do away with our gambling den and a number of parasites.
I should also like to see representatives of organized agriculture on all boards having to do with agricultural problems. For some time we have argued in favour of this procedure, and have consistently talked about it. I should hope the government would see fit to bring that policy into operation.
Canadian unity should be maintained, and the winning of the war should not be neglected to do any of the things I have mentioned. But the policy being handed out to agriculture to-day is forcing a large part of western Canada to a condition of starvation and relief.
With two verses from a poem entitled "When Babies Die," I would conclude. They are as follows:
The babies nazis kill:
Are they more dead Than those who perish in The days of peace,
Because that grasping fails To leave them food,
Because the greed of gold Knows no surcease ?
When nazi bombs are stilled,
And on the graves
0-f millions dead the wheat
Is Gold again,
Will man have learned a child Is just as dead By deprivation as By cannon slain?

Sing a song now.
Mr. JOHNSTON (Bow River) You don't understand it, anyway.
On motion of Mr. Wright the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on
Friday this bill was being discussed when the house adjourned at 6 o'clock, and at that time we were pointing out that we did not think the bill would be effective in solving the problem of reestablishing the soldiers in labour and
1154	COMMONS
Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
industry. Differences of opinion were expressed throughout the house as to whether industry recognized any responsibility to humanity, and as to whether the onus should be placed upon industry to take care of this problem. The bill when in force will attempt to compel industry to accept these men on their return.
I believe we can best judge the ability of industry to do that job properly by looking into its past history. Apparently those champions of industry who sit in the house cast aspersions on some of the statements I made, and suggested that I did not know much about it. Well, I spent some time over the week-end going through a report of the royal commission on price spreads, which was tabled in the house a few years ago, and I recommend this volume to the careful study of those persons who do not know what it contains. After having read five hundred pages of it I think they will agree with me that industry does not care very much for the welfare of the people generally in Canada who have their labour to sell. The main object of industry is to see how little it can pay labour to get the most work out of it, and to accept very little responsibility for the welfare of the people as a whole.
Industry in Canada has failed us in times of peace. I refer hon. members to page 118, where they will find this:
... in February, 1934, the average wage rate for all male workers was 10 cents per hour; where 93 per cent of all male workers in 1934 were paid less than the minimum rate for female workers; where, on a 55-hour basis, the average full time weekly earnings in 1934 for male and female employees was $5.72.
The whole record of this book is an utter condemnation of the place industry has played in the life of Canada.
Again, referring to the operations of certain chain stores, it says:
In fact the absence of any personal relationship between the central management which determines operating standards, and the employees in the stores tends to render, the central management oblivious to the human element involved in their policies. This was made obvious by the evidence given before the commission by the chief executive of one of the largest chains.
And so on, all the way through the story of 4he tobacco industry, the lumber industry, the itextile industry, production and distribution.
For more recent evidence as to the conduct <of industry in Canada we need to go back no farther than 1939. At that time, when Canada was expressing a need for war equipment, the government placed on the statute books a bill limiting armament profits to 5 per cent. In September the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) made the statement that although the department had appealed to the

patriotism of industry, it had been unsuccessful to the extent of being unable to place a single contract.
If we want something more recent respecting the attitude of industry, and particularly its attitude toward the very point with which we are now dealing, let me refer to information received from Kirkland Lake no less recently than last Friday, which tells of twenty-five ex-service men who have not been rehired merely because they took part in a strike to establish the right to collective bargaining through a union of their own choice. These men had had from two to eighteen years' service in the mine. Every one was an ex-service man, and in four cases their sons are in the army. I maintain and I repeat that I do not think industry has proved itself fit to solve a problem as important as this.
What we need is a complete survey of the raw materials and resources of this country and what the nation is going to need. That should have been taken before because we need it badly now, but we shall need it even more during the reconstruction period. Some form of planned economy should also be provided with the object of finding out what the main needs of the people of Canada are, what they are going to require in the way of food, clothing and shelter, and the making of decent homes. To correlate these two ideas may require some change in the status quo, perhaps some change in the motive which is the driving force of our economic and industrial life. The motive of service rather than of profit is one that should present itself to the government at the present time. Some privileges will have to be surrendered.
Labour will have to have its share in the industrial life and1 the machinery of production of this country. Labour must feel that the plant and machinery of production are something which it owns in part and that the resources of this dominion are the birthright of the Canadian people, not merely some privilege to be handed over to groups of selfish people to be exploited for profit. This bill does not begin to approach the large subject that lies underneath it. I do not blame the minister altogether for this. I think it is a sort of anaemic foundling which he found on his doorstep when he came into office.

speechtext:
I consider it a shame. Under previous legislation it was required that a person should have resided in Canada for some time prior to the great war to enjoy a preference in appointment to the civil service, and under that legislation the civil service has been filled with people who were not bom in this country and who are now occupying the finest positions in the land. Canada has become the dumping ground for all the nations of the world.
There is a distinction made in the legislation before us-and the minister was honest enough to admit it-between men and women. Men may come from all over the world to take advantage of this legislation and get something from this government, but for women service in his majesty's forces shall include service in the Canadian Women's Army Corps or in the Canadian Women's Auxiliary Air Force. There is a distinction clearly made between men and women, and how the minister can bring legislation like that before this house and this committee I cannot understand. He is a new minister, and I was quite open-minded because he was my colleague in the house for a certain length of time, but I cannot conceive that his idea of Canadian citizenship is that this country shall become the dumping ground of all the nations of the world and that it is to be enough for a man to get into his majesty's forces anywhere, in central Africa or anywhere else, to be entitled to the same privileges as a red-blooded Canadian who enlists in the Canadian army. This I cannot conceive to be right, and I do not know any Canadian citizen, born in Canada, who would pilot legislation like that through this house. I do not know any member who is not enough of a Canadian to protest strongly and bitterly against it until it is defeated in this committee and in this 
house. I have never before spoken like this, but it is time that we opened our eyes and stopped making fools of ourselves.

I might add that I have recently been through a by-election in Welland, and in speaking to the good people of that constituency I dwelt on the difficulty of governing a nation made up of all of the finest blood streams of Europe, including my own and my hon. friend's blood streams. My grandfather was a Frenchman and I am proud of it. At this very difficult time through which we are passing, when the very life of our institutions which it has taken centuries to build up is at stake, I do not think it is well that utterances should go forth from this House of Commons which would have for their purpose the splitting of this nation, not into two racial groups only, but into dozens of racial groups.
Whether my hon. friend likes it or not, the democratic nations of the world are in the most desperate position in their history. If we win this war it will be a miracle. But miracles have been performed by our peoples before and they will be undertaken by them again. In this very difficult period I do not think it lies in the mouth of any member of this house to rise in his place and cast reflections on men and women who have made a distinct contribution in building up this Dominion of Canada. I do not take second place to my hon. friend or anyone else in this house or in this dominion in loyalty to our institutions. I have been around this old world and have seen the institutions which have been built up by the British peoples. I believe that the science of government which

has been handed down to the rest of the world by the British peoples has been the greatest contribution to government in the whole history of the civilized world, and I hope that everyone in this dominion, irrespective of race, religion or colour, will do everything he can to help weld us together so that we may move forward through these difficult times to preserve and maintain our freedom and, when the war is over to extend the blessings of democratic government as we understand it.
I think my hon. friend misunderstands the tenor of the particular clause to which he refers, because it provides that a man must have worked in Canada before he can get the benefits of this legislation. I know some of our finest Canadian boys who at this moment are serving in the Royal Air Force and with the British navy and I think it is only right that these young men after they have completed their term of service should receive the same treatment, if they come within the four corners of this legislation, as those Canadians who join a distinctly Canadian force. That is elementary justice. We have always been credited with fairness and surely to God we are going to be fair to our own flesh and blood. We are not going to differentiate between them simply because some of our young fellows are serving in the British forces. If it were not for these young chaps up in an aeroplane to-day, this house would not be in session and probably I would be dead; I do not know what others would be doing. I think it is absolutely sound that we should treat these young men the same as we treat the young fellows who join distinctly Canadian forces, whether on the land or on the sea or in the air.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: The minister has forgotten the point raised by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. speechtext: Is that not a very technical interpretation?

speechtext: That is what I want cleared up. We have civil servants who have been employed for the last five years, but who are still temporary. On the other hand, a man or woman may be in some other job for only a month, yet he or she would be regarded as having a permanent position.

speechtext: Would this not be a fair thing to say about the civil service, that in the main you can almost call them permanent temporaries? subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Some of them have been temporary for twenty years.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES

speechtext:

this bill intended to cover not only those who have enlisted to date but also those who may enlist hereafter?

In order to prepare a foundation for my argument, I first point to line 6 of the preamble, which reads:
. . . and whereas many employers of persons who have enlisted to serve in his majesty's forces in the present war have voluntarily undertaken to reinstate in employment such persons . . .
Then at line 12:
. . . and whereas it is desirable that all persons who have left employment to enlist should be relieved of any cause for concern in regard to their reinstatement in such employment, and that there should be uniformity of treatment in the matter of reinstatement in employment of those who have so enlisted; and whereas it is deemed expedient for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada that provision should be made for the orderly reinstatement in their previous employment of such persons aforesaid . . .
In every case in the preamble reference is made to persons who have enlisted prior to this date. In no case in the preamble is there any reference to the necessity of protecting the men who enlist after this date. While ordinarily the preamble is not regarded as part of the statute, nevertheless it will be looked at in the matter of interpretation. The preamble definitely refers only to those persons who have enlisted to date.

now to the definition of service in his majesty's forces. It does not say what this means, but it does say what it includes:	It reads:
"service in his majesty's forces" includes service since the commencement of the present war in or out of Canada in any capacity, in pursuance of any enactment relating to the naval, military or air forces. . . .
That is service since the commencement of the present war.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES

speechtext:
I should
like first of all to refer to the parentage of this bill. On many occasions the minister has said that this measure was brought down in response to a promise made to me. speechtext: Would the minister indicate what benefit would accrue to a man who had enlisted, served in England for one or two years, and then was discharged within the last three, four or five months?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
