subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
Since this clause dealing specifically with the status of employees is to stand, I should like to make a few remarks now for the consideration of those who will be revising this clause.
As I see it, this bill has to do with one of the most important parts of rehabilitation,
how the man who leaves his job is to be placed when he returns. The minister of pensions said a moment or two ago that all or most of the legislation with respect to rehabilitation after the last war was left until the war was over. I know that many of us have grown old seeking legislation to try to cure some of the ills, physical and economic, suffered by the men who went through the last war.
What I am concerned about now is this. The economy of Canada to-day is geared to curtail as much as possible consumption buying and the production of consumer goods, in the course of which many peace-time industries are being legislated out of the picture. In the rubber industry, for example, I believe that thousands of workers will soon be out of work. These men will not have a job.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: The hon. member would not blame this legislation or government policy for that?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: No; lam simply pointing out what is happening. Many men employed in the rubber industry will be without a job through no fault of their own and through no fault of the minister, because he has no control over the shortage of rubber. These men will then have no status as an employee. Numbers of them will probably go into the armed forces in order to get a job, and when they return after the war is over, they will have no status as an employee when they enlisted. I leave that thought with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: They have all the other rights.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: They would have established employee status by being at work on September 9, 1939, or having been employed for six months after September 9.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
The retail gasoline industry is also being gradually legislated out of the picture. I know a lot of men who have enlisted and who had no status as an employee because the curtailment of their business forced them into unemployment. Having no status as an employee when they enlisted, they have no job under this bill when they return.
I have also in mind the men in Kirkland Lake who are unemployed to-day. Many of them since they became unemployed have perhaps already enlisted. They became unemployed because they obeyed the laws of Canada and accepted the government's proclamation by order in council that they had a right to do certain things and because the government urged them to organize and

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
cooperate with industry. Many of these men who will go into the armed forces have now no status as employees. As I pointed out in the few remarks I made on the second reading of the bill, I think it was a mistake to have separated this bill from the department of pensions. I think it should have stayed in that department and with the committee who have been working on rehabilitation in the past.
There is another class of worker for whom I would speak. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) referred to them a few moments ago. The men in the merchant marine are performing, I believe, one of the most essential war services to-day. We would have no war abroad if it were not for the service these men are performing. In the section from which I come many men have left industry and gone into the merchant marine. The}' have some protection if serving on a Canadian ship, but otherwise they have none. I have known of many ships which have docked in the port of Sydney and whose captains have had to go out and recruit men before they could take their ships out again. For patriotic reasons men have left their ordinary employment and gone into that service, and I think that under this bill they should have the same protection after the war as the men in the armed forces. There is not a man in uniform or out of it who is performing a greater service and getting as little for it as the men in the merchant marine. I take off my hat to them. They are performing one of the most vital services in connection with the war.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: They saved the army at Dunkirk.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Exactly, and they are now feeding the army, under difficult circumstances. It takes a lot of courage to get on these boats even when they are in harbour, let alone crossing the ocean. I make these remarks for the purpose of provoking the thoughts of the minister, so that when clause 2 is under revision consideration may be given to the points I haye raised.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
There is one point I should like the minister to clarify. He indicated very clearly the provisions of the order in council, but I have in mind several cases of men who enlisted one or two years ago in category A and have been discharged in category E. I referred one of these cases to one of the departments recently, but I do not know where it will be finally dealt with. These men will be going into hospitalization for six, eight or ten months, possibly a year.

When they come out, will they still be ' qualified to benefit under this bill, as and when it is passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I am not sure whether I caught the point.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: It will probably be a year before these men have recovered their health sufficiently, to get- into employment again. Will their employer then have to take them back?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: The point has not come to my attention before, but I would say yes.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: How can these men make application when in a state of convalescence except by anticipating their condition a year hence? The bill says that application must be made within a prescribed time.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Were they demobilized or discharged?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: The man I have in mind was discharged on the seventeenth of February.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: It would depend upon the interpretation of section 4, which says: "within three months after discharge". I would imagine that would only apply within three months after discharge from the forces. On the other hand, if the man were in one of our own hospitals awaiting discharge, he would apply within three months after discharge from the hospital.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Would he get hospitalization after discharge?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Well, then, he would not be covered.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Is that not a very important point, because many of these men who come back are not fit, and then they are discharged from the army and go under the Department of Pensions and National Health for treatment, and they are not able to work until they have completed that treatment? Surely section 4 should be amended to give the man three months, or whatever may be the time, after his discharge from the Department of Pensions and National Health.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
We have not yet reached section 4 of the bill. But I think the point is very well taken and that this should be clarified.
Section stands.

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
On section 3-Duty of employer to reinstate employee.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: This is the section which provides for reinstatement. It sets forth the duty of the employer to reinstate the employee, and there is a proviso which deals with the question of preserving the established rules of seniority in the employer's establishment. And it- '

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
And it leaves out pension
rights.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
It leaves
out pension rights. That is exactly what I am coming to. Suppose, for instance, a man has served for fifteen years in the employment of a particular firm and had established his right to pension in respect of that period of service; he then enlists, and at the conclusion of the war he returns to his previous employment. His pension rights are not preserved by the statute, and there is nothing in the statute which compels the employer to preserve the pension rights. He may have to begin over again. I do not know what the action would be on the part of an employer. To-day nearly every big establishment has some kind of a pension system. Some systems are contributory; some are not. I understand that all the railways now have contributory pension systems. A man has some vested rights there. I suggest that this section be redrafted to take care of pension rights just as much as seniority. It is very important to the men. I have often talked to railway men about their pension rights, and I do know that the older they grow, the more they value those rights. It is a kind of magna charta against old age. I should like to have the minister give attention to this question and let us have some undertaking with respect to it.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
The point raised by the
leader of the opposition is one to which I have given some thought. However, the phrase "conditions not less favourable" on page 2, line 30, of the bill, implies the retention of pension and other rights, and regulations can be made under authority of section 11, which could define conditions not less favourable, explicitly to include the retention of such rights. If the bill should specify the retention of pension rights, it might be construed to mean that other unspecified rights were not retained. It might, therefore, be advisable to leave such matters to regulations, especially since different arrangements would be necessary with respect to contributory and noncontributory pensions, sick benefit insurance plans and other plans. I think my hon. friend can rest assured that the matter will not be overlooked.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Well, if I were construing this, I would suggest that the clause in the earlier part of section 3 which the minister quoted, "and under conditions not less favourable to him than those which would have been applicable to him had he not enlisted", do not apply to questions of seniority and the like. They apply to his working conditions and his pay and emoluments, and contractual relationships which exist between the parties. Especially is authority given to that contention in the succeeding proviso, which is really not an overriding proviso at all, but is intended, I think, to be an extension of the clause that the minister quoted, "provided, that the right to reinstatement shall be subject to established rules of seniority in the employer's establishment". Under the ejusdem generis rule "pension rights" ought to go in there. I press for that. I am not sure that you can by regulation under section 11 force an employer to give the man a pension.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I want to say this to my hon. friend, that he is no more insistent than I would be that these men shall retain their pension rights.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
It is
important.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Yes; it is important. The lawyers tell me that if it is specifically mentioned there, you must mention all the other things like insurance and sick benefit funds.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I want to think about that a little. I want pensions in if I can get it in.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: As far as I am concerned it would be satisfactory to insert "pension rights" among the other rights specified.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
Well, you had better consider it overnight.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
